en: [Page 1] Homage to the upholders of the Anuyoga!
[Composed by the venerable teacher Vimala]
The Paümacariya:
A Discourse on the Abode of Liberation.
[The Auspicious Invocation:

I bow to Ṛṣabha, the bull among the best of Jinas, who is worshipped and highly honored by Siddhas, gods, Kinnaras, Uragas, Dānavas, and the lords of the Bhavanapatis; he is the first Tīrthaṃkara of this Avasarpiṇī age. (PaumaCariu 1)
Ajita, who has conquered the passions; Apunarbhava, the source of non-rebirth and the destroyer of existence;
Abhinandana and Sumati; Padmābha, who possesses the splendor of a lotus;
the Supreme One of the three worlds, Supārśva; Sasiprabha, the excellent Jina; and Kusumadanta.
Then [he praised] Śītala, the Lord of Sages; Śreyāṃsa and Vasupūjya;
Vimala and likewise Ananta; Dharma, the Jina who is the abode of righteousness; Śānti, the destroyer of the passions; Kunthu; and the highly fortunate Ara, the conqueror of enemies. (PaumaCa. 3–4)
I have honored Malli, who has crushed the stream of existence; Munisuvrata, of excellent conduct;
and the Lord of the Three Worlds, for it was at his *tīrtha* that this life-story of Padma arose.
I bow to Nami, Nemi, and likewise Pārśva, [whose teachings] shone like the jewels upon the great hoods of serpents. (Padma-Carita 5)
O Blessed One, I bow my head in homage to the Hero who has dissolved the impurity of passion and is saluted by the three worlds. (PaumaCa.
6) I also pay homage with my head to all those other great seers, the Gaṇadharas and ascetics who have attained majesty and are guarded in mind, speech, and body. (PaumaCa. 7)
[The subject matter:
All that is established in a succession of names, handed down through the lineage of the masters.
I shall relate the *Paumacariya* (The Deeds of Padma) in due order and in brief. (PaumCa.
8) Who is able to describe the entirety of the narrative of Padma’s life, except for the Kevalin Jina, who possesses knowledge of the three periods of time? (PaumCa. 9)
The meaning that emerged from the mouth of the Supreme Jina in manifold ways was retained by the Gaṇadharas; this [text] is its concise exposition.
Thus, through the succession [of teachers], there has been a decline in the original texts and their meanings. (PaumaCa. 10)
Knowing the nature of time, the wise person should not become angry. (PaumaCa.
11) There are some men here of uneven character who are intent on seizing faults; though they are pleased by well-spoken words, they do not acknowledge merit even when it exists. (PaumaCa. 12)
"Poets speak of the meaning expressed by the Omniscient One according to the qualities of their own tradition;
for does not a thread shine when pierced by a diamond needle?
In this very assembly, the minds of men possess many diverse variations. (PaumaCariya 13)
Who has ever grasped the [doctrinal] positions that have been carried away like leaves by the wind? (PaumaCa.

14) Even the Tīrthaṅkaras did not establish [this] as a single unified system; how much less could those like us, mere holders of the scriptures, do so—especially those of dull intellect? (PaumaCa. 15)
Even though people are indeed possessed of wrong views and are highly deceptive, hypocritical, and cunning, nevertheless I shall now speak according to the power of my own intelligence. (PaumaCa.
16) The body is filled with diseases, and life is as flickering as a flash of lightning; O Śiva, it is impermanent.
"Only so long as the taste of the *kavaka* fruit lasts, and for as long as the circle of the moon, sun, and planets endures.
Therefore, a man who seeks his own welfare must certainly cultivate within his heart the aspiration to praise the Great Beings. (PaumaCa. 17–18)
[The Fruitfulness of the Limbs of the Body:
Only those indeed are truly ears who are well-filled with the teaching of the Supreme Jina.
Like those of a jester, they were fashioned merely out of wood.
That alone is a true head which rolls about in the assembly of praise; any other, however, is devoid of merit and is like the hollow shell of a reed. (PaumaCa. 19–20)
Even those eyes which are intent upon the vision of the Jina are highly praised;

however, those clouded by false belief (mithyātva) are like those fashioned by a painter. Those teeth which are devoted to the discourses of the Supreme Jina possess a radiant luster. (Padma-Carita 21)
The rest [of the verses] are in the *śleṣaka* (punning) style, even though they have indeed been composed with verbal constraints (*vayaṇabandha*). (PaumaCa.
22) What can be done with a nose that is greedy for the scent of various fragrant flowers, yet does not know the fragrance of the well-sewn cloth in this world? (PaumaCa. 23)
Only those who speak with well-measured words are considered superior here;
others are like leeches, snakes, or frogs that merely lap up water.
That tongue which knows the essence of the doctrine is the beautiful one in the world. (Padmacarita 24)
The double-edged sword has a sharp blade, while the rest are like knives newly whetted. (PaumaCa.
25) Even that is considered superior: the lotus-face which is intent upon virtues; any other is called a mere vessel, filled only with tooth-germs. (PaumaCa. 26)
The man who studies and listens, and exerts himself in the ascetic life to the best of his ability, is indeed supreme in this world; any other, however, is merely a craftsman.
Thus, with great care, a man should abandon delusion.
It should be followed by one endowed with the intellect of policy and possessed of devotion to the teaching of the Jina. (PaumaCa.
28) Now, on this path composed by the eminent great elephant Vīra in the lofty *Paumacariya*, even today there is passage for the elephants among poets through its successive tradition. (PaumaCa. 29)
Just as a bee, greedy for the scent of ichor from the temples of elephants, proceeds along its path with its gaze fixed on drops of rutting-juice, so too have I set out by that very same way.
This work has been composed in verses (*gāhā*) according to the sequence of the Sūtras, rendered flavorful and with its meaning made clear and manifest. *Paumacariya* 30.1.
Listen to the *Paumacariya* in its abridged form, as told by Vimala.
(Paumacariya 31) [Table of Contents of the Work’s Subject Matter]

The duration of life, the origin of the lineage, the battle, the origin of Lavaṅkuśa, and the attainment of Nirvāṇa—these seven subjects, which lead to the cessation of rebirth, are the ancient themes here. This is the conduct of Padma; this is the cause, endowed with these subjects. (PaumaCa. 32)
Tisalāsuta said: "Listen briefly to the Sūtra.

[It concerns] the excellent place of Vīra on the summit of Mount Vipula, which is delightful to the mind; likewise, it tells in its entirety to King Śreṇika what was related by Indrabhūti. (PaumaCa. 33–34)

The origin of the lineage of the Kulakaras, the conduct that is the cause of the world, the birth of the Jina Ṛṣabha, and his consecration on Mount Mandara; [he taught] various instructions and the destruction of the suffering of the world. (PaumaCa. 35)
The emergence of universal omniscience, the showers of flowers from supernatural powers, the attainment of Nirvāṇa—the supreme bliss and majesty—honored by all gods and asuras;
likewise, the battle between Bharata and Bāhubalin exactly as it occurred. (PaumaCa. 36–37)
The origin of the Jātis and of those belonging to various heretical sects who assume diverse guises;
the origin of the lineage of the Vidyādharas and of Vijjudanta;
and also the terrible assault upon Saṃjayanta, the bull among the best of sages. (PaumaCariya 38)
The arising of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) and the mastery of flight through the power of the earth-mantra;
the birth of Ajita; and at the assembly (*samavasaraṇa*), the bestowal of both merit and demerit by the Vidyādhara, as well as the granting of refuge by the Lord of Rākṣasas. (PaumaCariya 39–40)

The gift bestowed by the Lord of the Rākṣasas, the granting of the boon, the origin of Prince Sagara, his suffering, his asceticism, and his attainment of nirvāṇa; [and] the passing away of Mahārakṣa and the narration of his birth and prosperity. *Padmacarita* 41.1.
Likewise, the continuation of the Rākṣasa lineage must be known;
and the origin of the Vānara dynasty, as well as the life-story of Taḍikeśin together with Udadhikumāra, should be understood in their proper sequence. (PaumaCariya 42–43)
The arrival and departure of the Kikkindha and Andhra kings, and the wrath of Vijayasīha against Aśanivega; PaumaCa.

Then, the entry into the city of Pātālākāra which brings blindness, the entry into Kikkindhipura on the delightful Mahendra mountain, and the arrival and entry into Laṅkā by the sons of Sukeśin, who were great in strength. (PaumaCa. 45)
The cause of Māli’s death by destruction and his vast current prosperity;
the birth of Indra in the city of Cakravāla on the southern ridge of the Vaitāḍhya range, and his sovereignty over the Vidyādhara ridges. (PaumaCa. 46–47)
The battle with Māli, the birth of Prince Vessamaṇa in the Kusumanta garden, and the entry of Sumāli’s son;
the union with Kekeyī by the thousands, and therein the manifestation of the supreme dreams. (PaumaCariya 48)
The birth of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa) and his acquisition of the vidyās;
the agitation of the Yakṣa Anādṛta, as well as the arrival of Sumāli and the obtaining of Mandodarī;
and the inspection of the maidens. (PaumaCariya 49–50)
Likewise, the life-story of Bhānukarṇa, the wrath arising from Vessamaṇa,
the battle between the Rākṣasas and Yakṣas, and the penance of Dhanada are to be known.
[PaumaCariya 51] The arrival of the Ten-faced one at Laṅkā, and his viewing and inquiry regarding the Jina temples.
And the life-story of Harisena, which is meritorious and likewise a destroyer of evil;

the capture of him who was named the Ornament of the Earth by the Great Intoxicated Elephant, and the place reached by Yama—the Sun, the Moon, and Kiskindhī—[all] devoid of constellations. (PaumaCariya 52–53)
The entry into the city of Pātālālaṅkāra, which was like a gateway to the destruction of the Daityas; the encounter with Suggīva’s splendor in the city of Virādha;
and the impact of the suffering of Anurādhā during the separation from Candōdaya—these he [experienced] in the city of Virādha, as well as the meeting with the glory of Suggīva. (PaumaCārita 54)
The destruction of Vālin at Mount Aṣṭāvata;
the recovery of Sītā by Suggīva and the death of Sāhasagati;
the supreme anguish of Daśamukha upon learning of the departure of Yaḍḍaka. (PaumaCārita 55–56)
The story of the birth of Aṇaraṇya and Sahasrakiraṇa, the destruction of Vairagya’s sacrifice, the account of their former births as bees, and the desire of Uvarambhā;
the acquisition of the sciences by Vijaya himself, and the destruction of King Mahendra’s fortune. *Padma-Carita* 57.
The journey to Mount Mandara, and the return once again;
the arising of omniscience for the great sage Anagāra of infinite power, the undertaking of religious vows by Rāvaṇa, and the birth of Hanumān. (PaumaCariya 58–59)
Above Aṭṭhāvaya, [he heard] Mahinda’s longing to see Palhāya, Pavaṇañjaya’s anger, and likewise his abandonment of Añjaṇā;
and the excellent sage related the entire account of the destruction of Haṇuya. (PaumaCa. 60)
And in the city of Haṇurūpa, there was a king named Paḍisūra;
in the middle of the Bhūyā forest, he placed Pavaṇañjaya the Khēyara under his command.
Likewise, [he experienced] the bliss of the festival of the vision [of the Jina], together with the ointment brought by the Vidyādharī;

and likewise the most terrible battle of the son of Pavanajaya, who possessed great strength, as well as the supreme sovereignty of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), and the interval between the two Victors (Jinas). (PaumaCariya 62–63)
The conduct of the enemies of Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, the accession to the kingdom of Daśaratha and his foremost sons,
the supreme prosperity of the lord of Kekeyī, the battle with Indra, and the seizure [of Laṅkā] by the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa)— [all these are told]. (PaumaCariu 64)
Overcome with spiritual agitation, the king attained the state of a renunciant. [PaumaCa.
65] The origin of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Sattrughna; the birth of Sītā in Videha, and likewise the connection to her grief. [PaumaCa. 66]

Having seen the delusion of his brother, who was licking the honeycomb of Nārada’s wife, he attained the supreme jewel of wisdom; and [he heard] of the renunciation of King Daśaratha at the feet of the refuge of the best of sages, Muṇisuvrata. (PaumaCa. 67)
The narration of those who have transcended existence, as well as the reunion with Sītā;
the recovery of Kekeyī’s son, the sovereignty of Bharata, and his supreme majesty;
likewise Lakṣmaṇa and Rāma, and how Sītā went to a foreign land. (PaumaCariya 68–69)
Likewise, the conduct of King Vajrakarṇa, the acquisition of the excellent Kumāra, Vasikāra,
Ruddhabhūti, and the liberation of Vālikhilya;
[and] near the rising of the sun, the most delightful settling of Rāmapura.
The union with Vaṇamālā, the attainment of supreme heroism, and the victory over Pauṣmā;

the overcoming of the afflictions of those who adorn their family and country, and the construction of a temple for the Jina by Rāma upon the summit of Mount Vaṃśa—these were his gains. (PaumaCariya 71–72)
Having witnessed the power of his gift, the dull-witted Jaṭāyu recognized his majesty as being solely derived from his restraint;
likewise, he observed the binding of Saṃbūka’s mouth and the arrival of Kekeyī’s sons, as well as the most terrible conflict with Khara and Dūṣaṇa. (PaumaCārita 73)
The grief of the divine Rāma was solely caused by the abduction of Sītā;
[he experienced] the swift arrival of Virādha, the slaying of Dūṣaṇa, the destruction of the jewel-adorned grove, and the meeting with Sugrīva. (PaumaCariya 74–75)
The slaying of Sāhasagati, the recovery of Sītā as the cause for the reversal of the cold [season], the meeting with Vihīṣaṇa, and the acquisition of the power of the *vidyā* Keśinī;
likewise, the supreme binding of Kumbhakarṇa and Indrajit by the serpent-nooses. (PaumaCārita 76)
The collection of the *Lakṣaṇasattis* and likewise the *Viśalyāgama*; the entry into the abode of the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), and the temple of the Lord Jina Śāntinātha.
*PadmaCarita* 77. [p.
Likewise, the manifestation of miraculous powers, the entry into Laṅkā, the appearance of the cakravartin, the death of the Ten-faced one at the hands of Lakṣmaṇa,
the lamentation of the excellent young women, and the arrival of the Kevalin. (PaumaCariya 78–79)
Likewise, [it describes] the initiation of those headed by Indradyumna, the meeting with Sītā, the arrival of Nārada and Lakṣmaṇa, and the entry into the city of Sāketa;
as well as the account of the previous births of Bharata and the others, exactly as it was narrated. (PaumaCariya 80)
Bharata took up the ascetic life, and Lakṣmaṇa was indeed established in the kingdom. (PaumaCa.
81) And though he had obtained the delightful [kingdom], death befell him—the one whose body was marked by the Śrīvatsa—in battle against the very great Rāvaṇa. (PaumaCa. 82)
The destruction of the afflictions for the country of the city of Mathurā, the arrival of the seventy sages, and the dwelling of Sītā;
then King Vajrajaṅgha sees Sītā and the birth of Lavaṅkuśa. *PadmaCariya 83*
Having conquered the lord of men, a battle was fought together with his father.

[Then followed] the arising of knowledge for those who are the ornaments of all people, the arrival of the gods, the account of the miraculous manifestations, and Sītā’s terrifying crossing of the ocean of existence. (PaumaCariya 84–85)
The terrible performance of penance, the anger at the self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara) at the word of Kṛtānta, the initiation of the princes, and the miserable rebirth of Bhāmaṇḍala;
the renunciation of Hanumat, and the cause for Lakṣmaṇa’s departure to the other world—[all these are told]. (PaumaCariya 86)

The penance of Lavaṇa and Aṅkuśa, the lamentation and grief of Rāma, which were produced by a deity from his previous birth; the renunciation of Rāghava, the attainment of unconditioned absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna), and likewise his departure to nirvāṇa. (PaumaCariu 87–88)
"May all noble and impartial people here listen thus to this path to perfection attained by Padma with a pure disposition. (PaumaCa.
89) This account of the eighth Rama-deva was told by Vira in the past; subsequently, it was maintained by the supreme *sādhus* and brought to light for the world.
Now, Vimala has composed this work in clear and manifest verses; may you now listen to this highly meritorious and pure-syllabled exposition of the Sūtra’s meaning.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Composition of the Sūtra" in the *Paumacariya*.
[The Genesis of Śreṇika’s Reflection] [The Magadha Country— ]

In this world of Jambudvīpa, in Dakkhiṇabharaḥ, there is a region named Magahā, endowed with great virtues, delightful, and adorned with cities and towns. It is strewn with villages, cities, hamlets, market towns, border towns, and ports. (PaumaCa. 1)
Abounding in cattle, buffaloes, and horses, its boundaries filled with heaps of wealth;
it was a multitude of pure people led by caravan-leaders, merchants, householders, and minor landowners, possessing great storehouses of jewels, gold, gems, pearls, and abundant grain. (PaumaCa. 2–3)
In that country, the people were skilled in various arts, possessed of exceedingly beautiful forms, endowed with strength, wealth, and splendor, and were especially devoted to righteousness;
it resounded with the constant sounds of actors, dancers, jesters, and musicians. (Padma-Carita 4)
With travelers being refreshed by various kinds of food, the city was even more intent on the preparations for the wedding festival;
it abounded in perfumes, flowers, and fragrant oils, and its energy increased incessantly through many drinks, snacks, and meals. (PaumaCariu 5.6)
[The city of Rājagṛha—] It was delightful on all sides with lotus ponds, lakes, and gardens; it was free from foreign armies, pestilence, thieves, and famine, and was full of joy. (PaumaCa. 7)
In its very center was an ancient city named Rājapura, surrounded by a vast and imposing wall.
It was free from any blemish, adorned with magnificent mansions, lofty archways, and white watchtowers. (PaumaCa. 8)

Furnished with iron bars, its upper stories adorned with golden ornaments, heavy with the weight of many precious goods, and its houses filled with gems flourishing both from the water and the land— *Padma-Carita* 9 [p. 9].
Resounding with the chatter of merchants gathered from various lands (PaumaCa.
10), and fragrant with the enjoyment of aloe, Turkish incense, and sandalwood, the courtyards of the palace were made radiant by the rays of emeralds and rubies during the dances (PaumaCa. 11).
Delightful with its temples, flourishing with groves, gardens, and forests, and possessing an exceedingly charming appearance from its lakes, ponds, pools, and reservoirs;
[the city] resounds with the great and sweet noise of spectacles at its crossroads and four-way junctions. (PaumaCa. 12)

Prosperous with wise people, possessing unerring conduct and many sacred texts—what need is there for much speaking? That city, an abode of thousands of virtues, was as if fashioned by taking the splendor of Amarapura itself. (PaumaCa. 13–14)
[King Śreṇika: "In such a city as this, there dwells a king named Śreṇika, endowed with the qualities of a monarch, like Vessavaṇa himself in person. (PaumaCa. 15)
With hair as black as bees, his facial beauty resembling that of a blooming, excellent lotus, with a neck thick, full, and firm, and endowed with slender, elevated, and long arms;
with a broad and wide chest, and a waist so slender and graceful it could be measured by the palms of the hands. (PaumaCariya 16)
His shanks were like the trunk of a lordly elephant, his thighs like the trunk of a pre-eminent elephant;
his beautiful feet were like those of a noble tortoise, shining like a golden mountain;
his face was as lovely as the moon, and he was as deep as the ocean. (PaumaCariya 17–18)
There was nothing that he did not know; the power of the king’s wisdom was such that his intellect had attained rightness, and he was capable of honoring his teachers and deities.
Even though he was a young man skilled in various arts and sciences, [he remained under the command] of that excellent king. (Padma-Carita 19)
Even if one were to speak for a very long time, one could not reach the end of his virtues. (PaumaCa.
20) [The Life of the Venerable Jina Śrī Vīra; The Birth of Jina Vīra and the Consecration Performed by the Gods.]
In this Bharahavāsa, there was a city named Kuṇḍaggāma, flourishing with virtues; and there dwelt a preeminent lord of men, Siddhattha by name. (PaumaCa.
And his wife, named Triśalā, endowed with many virtues and perfect in beauty—
into her womb the Jina entered at the final moment.
By the shaking of his throne, the gods, perceiving that the Lord of Jinas had been born...
Everyone set forth, their hair standing on end with joy. Having arrived at the city and performed a rain of fragrant water,
they took the Lord of Jinas and reached the summit of Mount Mandara.
Having seated him upon a lion-throne variegated with jewels on a pale-white stone slab, the lords of the gods consecrate him with jars of water from the Ocean of Milk.
And by him, Mount Meru was shaken sportively with his big toe. (PaumaCariya 25)
Therefore, the name Mahāvīra was bestowed upon him here by the lords of the gods.

Having bowed to the Lord of Jinas, having praised him, and having performed a circumambulation, the gods once again placed the Teacher of the Three Worlds in the care of his mother. (PaumaCariya 26–27)
Having been given food by the gods and having abandoned childhood through the consumption of ambrosial paste from their thumbs, the Jina reached the age of thirty. (PaumaCa.
28) [The renunciation, knowledge, and super-knowledges of Vīra.]

Then, on another occasion, the Hero, having understood the defects of the world and being filled with spiritual agitation (*saṃvega*), surrounded by the gods of the world, attained the state of renunciation.
Then, for him who was free from the eight karmas and absorbed in meditative concentration (*jhāṇa*): *Padma-Carita 29*
Kevala-jñāna, which illuminates the entire world, arose within him.

His blood was the color of milk, free from impurities and perspiration, and his body possessed fragrant scent, endowed with auspicious marks and qualities, exceedingly pure like the radiance of the sun. (Pauma-Cariya 30–31)
The eyes are motionless, the nails and hair are fixed and glossy; for a hundred yojanas all around, the region is free from pestilence. (PaumaCa. 32)
Wherever he places his feet, there spring up thousand-petaled lotuses; the trees become bowed with the weight of their fruit, and the earth becomes lush with crops.
The earth becomes like a mother, and here the Ardhamāgadhī language arises.
The quarters of the sky become as stainless as a lake, free from dust and pollen.
Wherever the Lord of Jinas stands, there appears a lion-throne adorned with jewels, enchanting for a league around, along with the sounding of drums and a rain of celestial flowers. (PaumaCa. 34–35)
Thus that bull among sages, the sun-like Lord of Jinas, dwells surrounded by the eight great miracles,
awakening the lotuses of those destined for liberation;
endowed with extraordinary splendor, he is accompanied by his retinue of the entire community, including the monks and the leaders of the order.

While dwelling there, the Great Hero reached the vast king of mountains. Accompanied by all the gods and asuras, Indra came to the vast mountain.

[The Praise of the Hero:
O Sun of the Rays of Kevala-Jñāna! In this entire world of living beings, which was blinded by the darkness of delusion and sleep, only you have illumined it with pure light. (PaumaCa. 43)

O you of great renown! You are a boat in the ocean of existence within saṃsāra, amidst the clashing waves of the great waters of suffering; you are the deliverer of the merchants who are the fortunate ones. (PaumaCa. 44)

O Lord! You have appeared as a caravan leader for those who have strayed onto evil paths within the thicket of worldly existence, that forest of trees consisting of the sorrows of union and separation.
O Lord! Who is capable of enumerating your truly existing virtues?
Even after being addressed for a long time— indeed, for thousands of millions of years—
the King of the Gods (Indra) and the other fourfold hosts of deities, having offered praise and prostrated with devotion, sat down in their respective positions. (Padma-Carita 46–47)

The King of Magadha also, having seen the arrival of the gods in the presence of the Jina with a great retinue of soldiers, departed from the royal city. Having reached that place, he dismounted from his excellent, rutting elephant.
Having paid homage to the Lord of Jinas, the Magadha feudatory sat down in his previously assigned place,
which was a circular expanse measuring one yojana in circumference. (Pauma-Cariu 49) [The Samavasaraṇa]
It possesses the beauty of expansive gopuras made of jewels, which are twice as high as the ramparts. (PaumaCa.
50) Furthermore, there are two Vakkhāra mountains, endowed with the eight great miracles;
and at each gate, the eight musical instruments dance. (PaumaCa. 51)

In the four intermediate directions and in the center, there are sixteen excellent ponds, each filled with pure water and lotuses and lilies; four in each direction. The Blessed One, the teacher of the three worlds, was seated comfortably upon a wonderful lion-throne.
Adorned with a succession of parasols, fly-whisks, *aśoka* trees, and a halo of light—[thus it was].
(PaumaCārita 53) In this manner, amidst that assembly of people gathered by the best of gods, I shall proclaim each of the Vakkhāra mountains individually. (PaumaCārita 54)

In the first pavilion, there was the assembly of the naked great seers (nirgrantha-maharṣi); immediately after that, in the second, [there was the assembly] of the many celestial women of the Sōdharma heaven and others. (PaumaCa. 55)
And on the third mountain range (Vakṣāra) is the assembly of the nuns of great virtue;

beyond that, however, is necessarily the assembly of the celestial maidens (Jyotiṣka-kanyās). Beyond that is the assembly of the Vidyādhara women, and then the assembly of the wives of the Bhavanavāsin gods.
Beyond that, however, there are necessarily the assemblies of the supreme gods of the Jyotiṣkas (luminaries), of the Vānavyantara and Bhavanapati lords, and in the Vakkhāra mountains;
thereafter, those of the gods dwelling in the Kalpas, beginning with Sōhamma. (PaumaCa. 57–58)
In the lower Vakkhāra mountain range is the assembly of humans and lords of men;
furthermore, in the northeastern sector is the assembly of animals. Thus, with their hearts serene, the multitude of kings gathered together with the foremost of the gods.
Having bowed to the Tīrthaṅkara, Gautama asks about dharma and adharma.
Then, with a voice as deep as a rain-cloud, the Lord of Jinas, generating benefit for all living beings, proclaims the Dharma in the Ardhamāgadhī language. (PaumaCa. 60–61)

[The teaching of the Blessed One, the Hero: "Substance is of two kinds; it should be known as living beings (jīva) and non-living beings (ajīva). Living beings are of two kinds: those who have attained perfection (siddha) and those who are in the cycle of existence (saṃsārin). (PaumaCa. 62)
For those who have become perfected beings (siddhas), there is infinite, incomparable, imperishable, eternal, and endless happiness, which is forever free from affliction. (PaumaCa.
63) Furthermore, those remaining in saṃsāra are to be known as twofold: mobile and immobile beings.

Both are of two kinds: mature (*paryāpta*) and immature (*aparyāpta*). Earth, water, fire, air, and plants are declared to be immobile beings (*sthāvara*). From the two-sensed up to the five-sensed, mobile beings (*trasa*) are of two types: those with consciousness (*saṃjñin*) and others [without consciousness]. (PaumaCariu 64–65)

That which is the non-living substance (ajīva-dravya), differentiated by the categories of dharma, adharma, and so forth, is the means for the attainment of liberation (siddhi-gamana) for those destined for existence; its opposite is for those not destined for existence. [PaumaCa. 66] Falsehood, the accumulation of activity (yoga), and likewise the passions (kaṣāya) accompanied by subtle vibrations (leśyā).
In these very [objects], the living being constantly binds unwholesome karma.
[But] through knowledge and vision, and through conduct accompanied by right austerity... [PaumaCa. 67]
One who guards their mind, speech, and body acquires infinite merit. (PaumaCa.
68) Karma, divided into eight types, has been briefly explained; through the yoga of transformation, living beings are both bound and liberated. (PaumaCa. 69)
The pleasure that arises for living beings deluded by attachment to sense objects— a pleasure lasting only a moment— is actually manifold suffering within this ocean of saṃsāra.
(PaumaCariya 70) Indeed, as long as time passes in the hell realm, even if it were measured by a mere blink of an eye...
There is not even that much happiness for living beings who have committed evil deeds. (PaumaCa.
71) In states of being tormented and beaten, and through the misfortunes of imprisonment and rebuke, animal-beings remain experiencing suffering. (PaumaCa. 72)
For human beings, suffering— both physical and mental— arises from union and separation, from gain and loss, and from passion and aversion.
(PaumaCariya 73) Even for gods of little power, it is seen when they behold the hosts of gods possessing great power.
Whatever suffering arises from that [birth], it becomes even heavier at the time of falling away.
In such a terrible saṃsāra, which is like a fourfold path, the living being, having merely fallen away from sufferings, finally attains human status. (PaumaCa. 74–75)

Even when human birth is attained, it is difficult for a living being to arise in a noble family; rather, birth occurs among the Śabara and other low-born families who possess little wealth. (PaumaCa.
76) Even if one is born into a good family, one may be a dwarf, deaf, blind, mute, crippled, or hunchbacked.
Through sufferings does a living being obtain a healthy form endowed with all five senses. (PaumaCa.
77) Even upon attaining union with all that is beautiful, one of little merit does not develop a sense for the Dharma; such a deluded person is overcome by greed and delusion. (PaumaCa. 78)
Even though an understanding has arisen regarding the Dharma as being superior to false doctrines and harmful practices, one is nevertheless still led astray;
such a person does not attain the Dharma taught by the Jina. Having obtained human birth, he whose mind is not always fixed upon the Dharma [is lost]. (Padma-Carita 79)
Indeed, for that man, his hand-like arm was destroyed by the nectar [of the poison]. (PaumaCa.
80) Who here are the wise men who, having taken up right conduct with true devotion, remained with their conduct unbroken until they reached the supreme forest? (PaumaCa. 81)
Furthermore,
some others, having meditated upon the twenty causes of a Jina— which cause the upheaval of the three worlds— attain infinite bliss. (PaumaCariya 82)
Having practiced distinguished austerity, with only two or three births remaining in their cycle of existence, they attain unsurpassed Nirvana.
Having performed noble austerity and perfected themselves through the power of their fortitude, they pass away.

They become the sovereign lords (Ahamindas) in the abodes of the supreme, unsurpassed celestial mansions. Having descended from there, and having enjoyed the prosperity and pleasures of the wielders of the plow and the wielders of the discus for a very long time, they practice the Dharma and attain perfection.

Having taken up the ascetic dharma, others—overcome by terrible hardships—forsake self-restraint and again practice the minor vows. Others become satisfied merely by the sight of the supreme lords of the Jinas. (Pauma-Cariya 86)
Having renounced [the world], they do not even return to it in their dreams. (PaumaCa.

87) Those whose minds are deluded by false belief, devoid of virtue, and lacking self-control, enter into the great and terrible fray of household life, lusting after the pleasures of the senses. (PaumaCa. 88)
Even those engaged in agriculture and various occupations that involve the oppression of many living beings go to hell, which is terrible and characterized by intense, great suffering. (PaumaCa.
89) Those whose nature is crooked with deceit, who employ false scales and false measures in their dealings...
Those who have no faith in the Dhamma fall into the animal realm. (PaumaCa.

Those who possess pure vision, knowledge, and conduct, who are free from attachment even toward the body through the mutual application of their means, attain perfection; having shaken off their karma, they reach that which is imperishable, infinite, unassailable, auspicious, and the supreme bliss. As many as there are lions among ascetics who have abandoned the foundations of karma, they attain liberation. (PaumaCa.
94) In the great ocean of the four states of existence, living beings whirl about, bound by their karma; none can cross over it except by means of the ship of the Jina’s Dharma. (PaumaCa. 95)
In the great summer heat of saṃsāra, which is scorched by the flames of the sun of suffering,
the entire world of living beings is cooled and refreshed by the cool rain-cloud of the Jina’s teaching.
(PaumaCariya 96) [Śreṇika’s doubt regarding the life of Padma].

98) Then, at the close of day, the sun indeed set;

It emits darkness into the sky, darkening the quarters of the horizon with its black hue;
thus is the nature of the wicked known, which extinguishes the light of the conduct of the virtuous.
Even the king, in his own palace, [remained] amidst the scattering rays of burning jewel-lamps.
Sleeping comfortably on a couch strewn with flowers, while enjoying his rest, he repeatedly saw the Lord of Jinas even in his dreams;
thereafter, he questioned him with great effort regarding his supreme doubt. (PaumaCa. 101–102)
Then the Great Soul arose, amidst the sound of many musical instruments and bards, accompanied by deep and resonant thunder-like roars, while being praised with hundreds of auspicious hymns.
(PaumaCariya 103)

105) It was solely through the religion of the Supreme Jina that those born of very great lineages became masters of all sciences; having reached the further shore [of knowledge], those heroes were filled with pride in their strength. (PaumaCa. 106)
The leaders of the world and all the Rākṣasas, headed by Rāvaṇa, give birth [to offspring] having made their food and drink of fat, blood, and flesh. (PaumaCariya 107).
It is said that the brother of Rāvaṇa was Kumbhakarṇa, who was possessed of great strength.
For six months, free from fear, he slept continuously upon beds. (PaumaCa.

He does not hear the sound of drums and kettledrums even when they are sounding right before him;
nor does that Great Soul rise from his bed at an improper time. Even if he has risen, his body is overcome by the terrible hunger for food. (PaumaCariya 110)
Whoever might be before him, he swallows elephants, buffaloes, and the like.
Having filled his belly with many gods, humans, elephants, and others, he ascends his bed once more and sleeps for six months, free from fear. (PaumaCa. 111–112)
Even Indra was heard of as having been conquered in battle by Rāvaṇa, bound in fetters, and brought to the city of Laṅkā.
Who in the three worlds, including the gods and demons, would be capable of conquering Indra? (PaumaCariya 113)
"He who uplifts Jambudvīpa, bounded by the ocean;

whose elephant-lord is Airāvaṇa, and whose thunderbolt is the weapon of unerring power—for him, even another [enemy], merely by being thought of, would surely turn into a heap of ashes. (PaumaCa. 114–115)

Just as a lion was slain by a deer and an elephant was routed by a dog, so too has the *Rāmāyaṇa* been composed by poets in a manner that is inverted and contrary to reality. All of this is false, for it is contradicted by logical reasoning, consistency, and the qualities [of the characters]. *PaumaCariu* 116.1.

117) Thinking thus, the king—his mind longing for the sight of the Jina and seeking a means to resolve his doubt—then conceived a desire to go. (PaumaCa. 118)

[Śreṇika’s visit to Gautama and his inquiry: Standing in the assembly hall, his body adorned with all ornaments, his turban made radiant by the rays from the pearls of the crowns of his vassal kings. (PaumaCa. 1)

There, the King of Magadha, eager for the sight of the Sage, mounted his excellent elephant, carrying in his hand the science of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śāstra*). Then he departed from the city, surrounded by noble elephants, chariots, warriors, and horses. (PaumaCa. 2)
The bull among kings went to where the Blessed Gautama was staying.
Having reached that place, in the midst of the assembly of the host of eminent sages, he beheld the bull among the *gaṇadharas*, like the autumnal sun in its splendor. (PaumaCa. 3–4)
Having dismounted from his excellent elephant and having circumambulated the sage, the king, with a joyful heart, bowed down while placing his hands joined in reverence upon his head.
Having been granted a blessing, he sat down at the feet of the best of sages. (PaumaCa. 5)
He inquired about his physical well-being with the utmost humility. (PaumaCa.
6) Having recognized the appropriate occasion, King [Sagara], once again endowed with humble courtesy, asked Gautama that which dispels the darkness of doubt. (PaumaCa. 7)
O you of great fame! I desire to hear the *Paumacariya* in its entirety, including the supernatural occurrences and those things that have been misrepresented by those who speak evil doctrines.
O you of great fame! If Rāvaṇa was a night-stalker of such exceeding prowess, like a preeminent god...
Who indeed was not overcome in the midst of battle by those who possess the nature of monkeys?
By Rāma, the golden-bodied Mārica was pierced with an arrow in the forest;
for the sake of Suggīva’s daughter, Vālin was slain through a stratagem. (PaumaCariu 9–10)
Having gone to the abode of the gods and defeated the Lord of the Suras in the midst of battle, he was bound with firm and hard fetters and cast into the prison-house. (PaumaCa. 11)
"Skilled in the art of saving his life, Kumbhakarṇa slept for six months;
how then was he bound by monkeys? It was as if he were a bridge over the waters of the ocean. "O Blessed One! Please show us favor and tell us [this], joined with its true meaning and its cause."
"Destroy the darkness of doubt with the light of knowledge.
(PaumaCariya 13) Then the Lord of the Gaṇadharas said: "Listen, O bull among men! With your ears and mind attentive, I too shall relate to you that which was taught by the Kevalins. (PaumaCariya 14)
"He is not called a Rākṣasa, nor is Daśānana a consumer of raw flesh; all this which the foolish poets speak is false. (PaumaCa.
15) "Furthermore, [a composition] devoid of the 'pillow-band' (*pīṭhabandha*) does not convey its true meaning, even if it is being recited."
"O King, this speech is base and its root is severed, as it were.
First, I shall describe the division of the fields and the division of time therein; then listen to the life-stories of the great Great Beings in their proper order. (PaumaCa. 16–17)
[The World:
There exists infinite-infinite space; in the midst of that is the world, which is without beginning or end, eternal, and divided into three parts. (PaumaCa. 18)
The world should be known as being like a *vēttāsaṇa* (a type of seat), with its middle part resembling a *jhallarī* (a small drum) and its upper part having the shape of a *muraya* (a large drum).
Furthermore, it is like a palm tree (*tāla*), being encircled by three folds. (PaumaCa. 19)
In the center of the horizontal world (tiryagloka), amidst many oceans and islands, [is Jambūdvīpa].
And in its central region is Jambūdvīpa, which has the shape of a mirror.
And it measures one hundred thousand yojanas in circumference.
Furthermore, it is entirely surrounded on all sides by the salt ocean and by a magnificent jewel-lotus fence, which possesses a radiant splendor at its gates. (PaumaCa. 21–22)
In the center is Mount Mandara, adorned with four groves and variegated with jewels;
it rises ninety-nine thousand [yojanas] and extends ten [thousand]. (PaumaCa.
One thousand yojanas deep, it rests against the diamond layer below and touches the Saudharma heaven above at its crest; furthermore,
there are six mountain ranges that serve as rain-shelters, and seven rain-regions are to be known.
There are fourteen great rivers and four Nābhi mountains;
twenty Vakkhāra mountains and thirty-four royal capitals; likewise, the Veyaddha and Savaya mountains are to be known as thirty-four each. (PaumaCa. 25–26)
Likewise, there are sixty-eight caves and thirty lion-thrones for the Uttarakurus; in the center, under the excellent tree, is the celestial [palace]. (PaumaCa.
27) It should be known that there are two hundred golden peaks and six lakes.
Cittavicittā and Yamalagiri are the two [mountains];
there are six divisions of pleasure-lands, adorned with excellent trees and delightful to the mind.
And in these places, there are temples of the Jinas. (PaumaCa. 28–29)
Now, beyond this salt ocean, four islands are to be known;
they are beautiful with Jina temples and, in their enjoyment, equal to the celestial realms.
On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the southern part of Bharata, there is the island of the Rākṣasas.
Dīva is to the south of Gandhavāṇa and stands to the west of Videha;
Eravaya is to the north of that, and Kinnaradīva lies to the east of Pūrvavideha; furthermore, Varuṇadīva stands to the south of Pūrvavideha. (PaumaCa. 31–32)
In Bharata and Airāvata, decrease and increase occur; in the remaining regions, time remains eternally constant throughout the lands. (PaumaCa. 33)

The lord of Jambudvīpa, Anādṛta, a god of great power accompanied by thousands of deities, exercises sovereignty over all of them. Formerly, this Bharata was filled with enjoyments equal to those of Uttarakuru. (PaumaCa. 34)
In those most excellent and perfectly equal aeons, it is exceedingly beautiful. (PaumaCa.
35) The height of those humans is exactly three *gavyūtas*, their bodily configuration is square, and their lifespan is three *palyopamas*. (PaumaCa. 36)

The wish-fulfilling tree has musical instruments as its limbs, food as its coals, ornaments as its embers, garments as its fuel, the house as its flame, the lamp as its light, vessels as its ashes, and garlands as its roots. (PaumaCa. 37)
With these [five senses], they enjoy tenfold great pleasures that are delightful to the mind and according to their desire, always happy; even when their life has passed, they do not know it.

Then, having passed away, they obtain the happiness of the foremost gods.
Even lions and other [beasts] become gentle; they do not harm one another, sporting according to their own will in pleasure, and they too indeed enjoy happiness. (PaumaCa. 39–40)

however, in the remaining regions, there is neither decrease nor increase.
Having heard this, the king, having bowed again to the sage, questioned him further.

"For what reason is a human being reborn in the lands of enjoyment? [Thus asked. Then the Lord of the Gaṇadharas replied: "Those noble men here who are upright attain the path to the lands of enjoyment by means of giving to the virtuous. (PaumaCa. 42–43)
[The Fruit of Giving:
Those who give gifts to unworthy recipients for the sake of attaining pleasant enjoyments are born as elephants and experience the happiness resulting from that giving in this world. (PaumaCa. 44)

Just as a seed sown in well-tilled soil flourishes and does not diminish, so too, by giving to a virtuous ascetic, one accumulates vast merit. (Pauma-Cariu 45) Just as water drunk by a cow from a single pond [is multiplied], whereas that drunk by a snake...
Poison transforms into nectar in snakes, and milk arises from cows;

likewise, a gift given to one who lacks virtue and to one who possesses great virtue will bear fruit or be fruitless in the next world, according to the excellence of the recipient, so too is his merit. (PaumaCa. 46–47)

[The conduct of the Kulakaras and Ṛṣabhasvāmin: "Thus, O King, I have described in brief the excellence of giving, the lineage of the Kulakaras, and their origin; now I shall speak—listen! (PaumaCa. 48)
Just as the moon waxes and wanes by its own nature, so too does the *utsarpiṇī* increase and the *avasarpiṇī* decrease. (PaumaCa. 49)
In the third period of time, when eight parts of a *palyopama* remained, the first Kulakara bull, named Śatadru, appeared.
He was a great soul who remembered his births and knew three previous lifetimes. (PaumaCa. 50)
And because his faith was serene, the entire earth dwelt happily everywhere. (PaumaCa.
51) Thus, when time had passed, Sammūī was born next; then Khemankara was born, and after him, Khemandhara was born. (PaumaCa. 52)
The great-souled Sīmaṃkara was born, then Sīmaṃdhara, Payāṇanda, and thereafter the one named Caraka; they were all born in the land of Bhārata. (PaumaCa.
53) He by whom people, terrified upon seeing the moon and the sun, were comforted.

The abode of the state of enjoyment, where Nābhi himself dwells, is [the city of Ayodhyā]. (PaumaCa.
57) His wife, endowed with many virtues and possessed of youth, beauty, and form, was named Marudevī; she was like a goddess manifest before his eyes. (PaumaCa. 58)
The goddesses Hri, Śrī, Dhṛti, Kīrti, Buddhi, and Lakṣmī constantly carry out those very services for him at the command of Indra,
providing food, drink, sandalwood paste, bedding, seats, bathing, and other necessities. (PaumaCariu 59)

The divine beings sang, as did the lutes, celestial musicians, and dancers. (PaumaCariya 60) Then, on another occasion, while sleeping comfortably on a costly bed during the latter part of the night, Marudevi saw auspicious dreams. (PaumaCariya 61)

At the conclusion of the dream, amidst the sound of musical instruments resounded by the shouts of "Victory!",
she blossomed like a lotus-pond at the arrival of the sun; having performed the rites of purification, her eyes filled with joy,

"How many [Tīrthaṅkaras] have already passed, and how many great beings will there be? (PaumaCa. 143).
The Tīrthaṅkaras, Cakravartins, Baladevas, and Vāsudevas. (PaumaCa. 144) [Tīrthaṅkaras—]

The Jina spoke with longing: "Rishabha by name was the first Tīrthaṅkara, by whom here in the land of Bharata the Dharma was taught to the world. Having established his son in the kingdom and having taken up the ascetic life, he passed away. (PaumaCa. 145)
And the one currently existing, Ajita—by him I am equal. (PaumaCa.
146) Likewise Saṃbhava, Abhinandana, Sumati, Padmaprabha, Supārśva, Candra, Puṣpadanta, Śītala, and Vāsupūjya. (PaumaCa. 147)
Vimala, Ananta, Dharma, Śānti, Kunthu, Ara, Malli,
Munisuvrata, Nami, Nemi, Pārśva, and Vīra are the Tīrthaṅkaras.
These twenty-two Jinas will appear in due order in the future time.
Their protectors were Cakkavaṭṭī, Santī, Kunthū, and Ara. (PaumaCa.
149) Born into the most excellent families, all were consecrated with the milk-ocean water;
all indeed went to liberation, and all became possessors of kevala-knowledge. (PaumaCa. 150)
These twenty-four Jinas, the supreme ones in the world, have been declared by name; listen, O Cakravartin, as I shall proclaim them in their proper order. (PaumaCa.
151) [The Cakravartins—]
Bharata was a universal monarch (cakravartin) in the past; now you are Sagara; and the remaining wheel-turning kings will arise in the future time. [They are:
Maghavan, Sanatkumāra, Śānti, Kunthu, Ara, and Subhūma.
Pauma (Padma), Harisena by name, Jayasena, and Bambhadatta;
Acala, Vijaya, Bhadra, Suprabha, and Sudarśana should be known;
Ānanda, Nandana, Pauma (Padma), and the ninth is Rāma, who is Baladeva.
He shall be Tiviṭṭha (1), Duviṭṭha (2), Saṃbhū (3), Purisottama (4), Purisasiṃha (5),
Purisavarapuṇḍarīka (6), Datta (7), Nārāyaṇa (8), and Kaṇha (9).
[PaumaCariya 155] The first shall be Āsaggīva (1), then Tāraga (2), Mēraga (3), Niśumbha (4), and Mahukēṭabha (5).
Bali, Palhāo, Rāvaṇa, and likewise Jarāsindhu were adversaries.
These highly noble men existed during the period of the *avasarpinī*;
and again, there will be just as many during the *utsarpinī* period as well. (PaumaCariya 156–157)
Having practiced the Dharma taught by the supreme Jina with fivefold devotion, men such as these, having become so, attain supreme peace. (PaumaCa. 158)
But those living beings who are devoid of Dharma and bound by many evil karmas,
they wander through the wilderness of saṃsāra, which is expanded across the four realms of existence.
Having thus heard the nature of time and the accounts of great men, [one should reflect upon them].
Ghanavāhana attained detachment in that very instant. (PaumaCa.
160) By one deluded by the objects of the five senses and whose mind was overcome by passion for his beloved, even the Dharma was not practiced; alas! Woe! I have deceived myself. (PaumaCa. 161)

Who indeed, if he were a conscious man, would find delight in life, which is like a rainbow in a dream and as flickering and transient as a flash of lightning? Therefore, having abandoned kingdom, wife, sons, and wealth— wealth indeed!— *Padmacarita 16.2*
"I take up the Dharma, the supreme kinsman, which provides security for the next world. (PaumaCa.
163) Having consecrated his eldest son, Mahārakkhasa, upon the throne, that steadfast one, having cast off all attachments, entered the life of a renunciant. (PaumaCa. 164)

In the city of Laṅkā, the Lord, the son of Ghanavāhana, whose fame is spread abroad, the king of the Vidyādharas, enjoys sovereignty like a supreme god. His wife is Vimalābhā; from her, sons were born in succession. *Padma-Carita* 165.5.
The first was Devarakṣa, then Udadhi, and Ādiccarakṣa;
then Ajita Jinendra, having shown the path of Dharma to the world, attained the supreme, eternal state of liberation on the peak of Mount Sammeta. (PaumaCa. 166–167)

[Sagara’s sons’ pilgrimage to the eight-fold path and their burning by the lord of the Nāgas —] Sagara, too, as a universal monarch, enjoyed sole sovereignty over this entire and powerful Bhārata, his splendor augmented by sixty-four thousand young women. (PaumaCa. 168)
Sixty thousand sons, resembling the form of the Lord of the Immortals (Indra), were born on the Aṣṭāpada mountain; they arrived there for the purpose of paying homage.
Then those lions among princes praised the temple-palaces; it was reported to them by their ministers that these had been caused to be built by Bharata.
"Quickly devise some means here for the sake of protection! (PaumaCa.
171) Then, having struck with the jewel-staff in the middle of the Ganges river, the son of the ocean surrounded the mountain with a moat. (PaumaCa. 172)
And having seen that opening, the lord of the nāgas, burning with the fire of pride,
became enraged and instantly consumed all his sons;
yet he did not burn the two eyes situated between those princes.

Having shown compassion through the power of the religion of the Supreme Jina, and having granted this death to his sons, the one who had conquered all enemies arrived at the city of Sāketā together with Bhaīrahībhīma. (PaumaCa. 174–175)
As they were about to descend into the ocean, those ministers— experts in the science of policy— suddenly restrained them from that terrifying whirlpool of death.
Having gone there, those excellent ministers bowed to the Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin).
Seated upon the offered seat and having made her resolve, she began to speak:
"Behold here, O King, the impermanence and worthlessness of this world!
What wise man in this world would feel grief for it? (PaumaCa. 177–178)

In former times there was a wheel-turning monarch named Bharata, whose power was equal to yours; by him this earth, consisting of six regions, was brought under control like a maidservant. *Padma-Carita* 179.
He had an eldest son, renowned by the name Ādityajasas.
And in this world, there exists a lineage renowned by name.
In this royal lineage, which is endowed with power, prosperity, and fame, many kings have passed away after exercising great sovereignty for a long period of time. (PaumaCariya 180–181)
Let humans wait; even those lords of the gods, possessed of great power and blazing with wealth, are like extinguished fires.
Even those bulls among the best of Jinas, whose soles of the feet are bowed to by the entire world—*Padma-Carita* 182.2.
When the destruction of their lifespan has arrived, even they abandon their bodies. (PaumaCa.
183) Just as birds, having dwelt upon a single great tree, depart toward the ten directions at dawn, so too do living beings [separate] from a single family. (PaumaCa. 184)
The associations with beloved people, as well as the wealth and bodies of living beings, are like rainbows, foam, dreams, flashes of lightning, flowers, and bubbles.
Even those who dry up the oceans and shatter Mount Meru with their fists, [are subject to this]. (Padma-Carita 185)
In due course, those men too entered the very mouth of Death.
In the world of the living, death is the most powerful of all things, however strong they may be.
By whom infinite wheel-turning monarchs and others here have been led to their final end. (PaumaCa.
187) Thus, in this world including gods, asuras, and humans, which has fallen under the sway of death, only the Siddhas—who have cast off the defilement of karma—are truly at ease. (PaumaCa. 188)

When the life-story of these beings born of noble lineage, who were abodes of thousands of virtues, is remembered, how indeed would the heart not burst? Just as those kings in due course attained their end here in this human existence— *Padma-Carita* 189.
"In the same way, we all shall also depart without hesitation. (PaumaCa.
19) "Listen further, O Lord! You see both of these with dejected faces and terrifying cries;
surely the rest have met their destruction. (PaumaCa. 191)
Having seen that and hearing of the death of his own son, the king—
his limbs pierced by the dart of intense grief and rendered senseless by a swoon— fell down.
His body sprinkled with sandalwood water, he regained consciousness from the suffering caused by his son's death.
Then he began to lament, shedding a flood of tears from his eyes:

"Alas! My sons, whose bodies were so delicate and who possessed forms like those of the gods—by whom have they been destroyed so suddenly, though they had never offended any wicked enemy? (PaumaCariya 193–194)
"Alas! O abode of a thousand virtues! Alas! O you of supreme form, with a face as lovely as the moon!
Alas! By cruel and pitiless Fate, you have been carried away from me.
O wicked Fate! Do you have no children who are dear to your heart? (PaumaCariya 195)
"By whom you have here slaughtered my sons, thousands upon thousands.
Having lamented these and many other words, the Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin), having become awakened and filled with spiritual agitation, then spoke. (PaumaCa. 196–197)
Alas! While deluded by sense-objects and bound by the rope of affection for my kinsmen, I, unfortunate in my youth, did not practice the Dharma.
What use have I for the earth, even if it were filled with the nine treasures along with their jewels? (PaumaCa. 198)
That I do not behold the faces of my sons, who have attained what is so difficult to find.
Fortunate are those true men, Bharata and the others, who, having renounced the earth, became mendicants out of detachment from sensual enjoyments and free from worldly ties. (PaumaCariya 199–20)
Then he, having consecrated Bhagīrathī—
the son of Jahnu— who was equal to Bhīmaratha, in the kingdom, went forth into the religious life in the presence of the Best of Jinas.
(PaumaCariya 201)
Having performed noble austerity and having attained omniscience (*kevala*) together with his son,
the great-souled Sagara reached liberation (*siddhi*) at the end of his lifespan.
Then Bhagirathi also ruled the kingdom, surrounded by a multitude of great warriors.
In that excellent city of Sākeya, as Indra is in the city of the gods.
[The previous birth of Bhagīratha:
Then, at one time, Bhagīratha, having gone and paid homage to the bull among sages...

Having settled right there and heard the Dharma from one who was not far away, the noble youth Bhagirathi questioned that ocean of learning, the monk: "For what reason are these two among them not dead? (PaumaCa. 204–205)
Then that best of sages said, "Let us go to Mount Sammeta.
Traveling slowly as he wandered, he reached the last village.
Upon seeing the community of ascetics, the villagers of that place began to harass them. (PaumaCa. 206)

Forbidden by the potter and reviled with harsh words, he took up the life of a thief. There, a certain man living in a village committed an offense against him, and for that reason, the king burned the village. (PaumaCa. 207–208)
The potter also went at that time to another village; there he was alone, and by the power of his karma, he was not burned.
Having died, the potter was reborn as a merchant, prosperous with great wealth.
From there, having passed away together with him, he became a village in Vārāḍaya.
Then, having died even from that state, he was reborn as a merchant and a king;
the villages also, being trampled by elephants, became the wives of Mātali. (PaumaCa. 210–211)
"O King, having become a śramaṇa, he became a god in an excellent celestial vehicle (*vimāna*); having fallen from there, you were born as King Bhagīratha.
As for those village folk, having met their death, they passed through various births. — *Paumacariya* 212.2.
The sons of Sagara were born produced by the power of their past karma. (PaumaCa.
213) The man who, bound by passion and hatred, utters reproach against the Saṅgha, wanders repeatedly through the terrible cycle of existence for thousands of births. (PaumaCa. 214)
Having heard his own life story and the cycle of existences of his sons,
Bhagirathi became a monk and after a long time attained perfection. This life story of Sayara, which arose in former times, has been narrated to you.
Henceforth, O lord of men, listen to that which has been requested by you. (PaumaCārita 216) [The world-weariness of the great rākṣasa and his former birth— ]

There, that great-souled one, the lord of the people of Laṅkā, the great Rākṣasa, enjoys a kingdom of great splendor, free from thorns and favorable. One day, surrounded by young women, he was in a magnificent garden. (PaumaCa. 217)
Having sported in the waters of the lotus pond, he sees a bee in the midst of a lotus.
Just as the ignorant bee, greedy for the fragrance of the lotus, perishes, so too have I perished, being solely attached to the lotus-like faces of young women. (PaumaCa. 218–219)
Devoid of right understanding, even bees inevitably perish; since even a skillful one has perished, that was surely due to the intoxication of delusion. (PaumaCa.
220) If this bee has met its destruction merely by [the lure of] fragrance and flavor, then...
"I was ruined from the very beginning, for I was subject to the power of the five senses.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of the senses, a man who is devoid of Dharma wanders through the long cycle of saṃsāra, which has four ends, again and again. (PaumaCa. 221–222)

While the Lord of Laṅkā remained reflecting with a detached disposition, the ascetic Suyasāgara, surrounded by his community, arrived at a safe stone slab in a garden free from living beings and creatures. (PaumaCa. 223)

Right there he settled down, engaged in religious duties together with the ascetics. (PaumaCa. 224) Then, when the garden-keepers announced the arrival of the ascetics, the king went forth with a devoted mind and paid homage to the Sage, that ocean of sacred knowledge. (PaumaCa. 225)
Having prostrated in due order before the rest of the community of ascetics,
the king sat down and questioned the lord of sages regarding his own cycle of existences. Then the ascetic began to explain, by means of the scope of his fourfold knowledge (*caturvidhajñāna*).
In this city of Poyanapura, there lived a man named Hiya-kara;
his wife was Mādhavī, and their son was you, Pōyaṅkara.
There, King Hēmaraha became devoted to the religion of the Jina. (PaumaCa. 227–228)
On another occasion, having performed worship at the shrine with devotion, he raised a cry of victory for the Supreme Jina, accompanied by the sounds of drums and conchs. (PaumaCariya 229)
Having risen as soon as he heard the sound, with a heart joyful and delighted, he then began to proclaim the auspicious hymn of praise for the Jina.
Having passed away from there, he became a Yakṣa endowed with great supernatural power. (PaumaCa. 230)
In the lower Videha, in the city of Kañcana, he saw a supreme ordeal being inflicted upon the best of sages.
Having warded it off by his power, the Yakṣa protected the body of the supreme sage and accumulated merit. (PaumaCa. 231–232)
Then, having descended, he was born as the son of Queen Śrīṛṣabhā on Mount Veyaddha, belonging to the Taḍiyaṅgaya Khecaras; he became a noble prince.
Then, while going for worship, he beheld the movement of the Cāraṇas. (PaumaCa. 233)
Then that fool, proud of his mastery of the sciences (*vijjā*), made a vow (*niyāṇa*):
"Having performed extensive austerity, may I become a preeminent god in the realm of Īśāna.
Having been born as the son of Ghanavāhana, you have now become the great Rākṣasa, Mahārakṣa. (PaumaCa. 234–235)
"There is no satiety in the enjoyment of fragrances; since you, O bull, have not gone [to them] for a very long time, how will you be satisfied with only a sixteenth part of a day?
Having heard these words, the great bull then fell into despair.
The king, whose state was such that death was near, spoke these words:
“Deluded by the poison of sensual pleasures and impassioned by love and affection for women, I did not even realize how much time had already passed. (PaumaCa. 237–238)
When a house is on fire, a well cannot be dug by those who are already suffering; likewise, a horse that has bolted cannot be tamed once it has been pursued.
Having anointed his son Devarakkhasa in the kingdom, the king— *Padma-Carita* 239ab.
Likewise, having installed Bhānura-kkhasa on the position of crown prince, he went forth into the religious life.
Having renounced all attachments and abandoned the fourfold food, he passed away through the practice of *ārāhaṇā* and became a supreme deity. (PaumaCa. 240–241)
In the city of Kinnaragīya, there was a daughter of the Vidyādhara Śrīdhara named Raivega; she [became] the wife of Devarakṣa.
In the city of Gandharvagīta, [she became the wife] of the king named Surasannibha.

Jāyā, the daughter of Gandhāri, was born as the wife of Bhāṇurakkhasa. PaumaCa.243 Ten sons of the gods and rākṣasas were born, and likewise six excellent daughters were born to Bhāṇurakkhasa; just as many [as the sons] were produced. PaumaCa.244
[55] The excellent cities, resembling the city of the immortals and possessing names similar to their own, were quickly made by the sons of the Rākṣasa with many settlements. (PaumaCa. 245)

By name they are: Saṃjhāyāla, Suvēla, Maṇapalhāya, Maṇōhara, Haṃsaddīva, Harija, Dhanna, Kaṇaya, and Samudda; and the tenth is Addhasagga—these are the settlements, flourishing with great virtues. (PaumaCa. 246)
The powerful [clouds] were produced by the sons of the great Rākṣasa Mahābala;

they had swirling, vast clouds, fierce and manifestly difficult to grasp, and being highly fortunate, their jewels were turned back by the heat of the sun by the sons of the Rākṣasa Ravi. (PaumaCa. 247–248)
The settlements of the sons of the Rākṣasas shine, illuminated by the mass of rays from various kinds of jewels on the lofty archways of their excellent palaces;
they serve as playgrounds for the sons of the Rākṣasas.
King Devarakṣa is the first, while Bhānurakṣasa is the second king.
Having taken the supreme initiation, he attained a state free from affliction.
Thus, when that great lineage had passed away, Mehavāhana was born.
The great-souled son of Rākṣasa was born of Maṇavegā.
By his name, this lineage of Rākṣasas became renowned in the world.
From him also was born Ādityagati, who possessed great fame. (PaumaCariya 251–252)
The sons of Queen Suprabhādevī, excellent youths with a radiance equal to the sun and moon, became ascetics for a long time; their father, however, went to heaven.
Their mother was named Madanapadmā, the beloved wife of Ādityagati. (PaumaCariya 253)
A woman named Āuṇahā was born to Mahantakitti, the son of Āiccagai.
To him was born a king named Bhīmaraha, who had one thousand excellent women as his wives. (PaumaCa. 254–255)
Having taken up the ascetic life along with one hundred and eight sons who resembled the forms of immortals, Bhīmaratha set forth toward perfection.
Indeed, the Rākṣasas guard the islands which are protected by merit. (Pauma-Cariya 256)
For that very reason, the name "Rākṣasa" was given to the sky-dwellers by the world. This origin of yours as a Rākṣasa-king has been recounted to you.
Listen now, Sreṇika, to the lineage of men in brief: PaumaCa. 258.
The first son of Bhīmaprabha, worthy of honor, was born; having established Jitabhānu upon the throne, he went forth as a renunciant of renowned glory. PaumaCa. 259.
The son of Jitabāṇu will be Saṃparikīrti; his son will be Viśālavakṣala;
his son will be Suggīva; and his son will be Harigīva.
Then there will be Śrīgīva, Sumukha, Suvarṇa, and the one named Amitavega.
Āiccagai, Kumāra, Indappabha, Indameha, Jāta, Mayāridamana, Pahiya, Indai, Subhāṇu, Dhamma, Surāri, Tijaḍa, Mahaṇa, Aṅgāra, and Ravi—these are the Āditya-gati-kumāras. (PaumaCa. 261–262)

He whose center is the wheel, who possesses the joy of the excellent lion-vehicle, who is heroic and has the fourfold roar, who is formidable, the bringer of fear to his enemies, the slayer of foes, devoted to Nirvāṇa, of fierce glory, and devoted to Arhatship. (PaumaCa.
Likewise, Pavaṇuttaragati, Uttama, Anila, Caṇḍa,
Laṅkāsoga, Mayūha, Mahābāhu, Manorama, Raviteja, Mahagati, Mahākāntayaśas, and Ari-saṃtrāsa were the kings. (PaumaCariya 264–265)
Candravadana, Maharava, Meghajnana,
as well as Grahakshobha, Nakshatradamana, and others— thus are the Vidyadharas to be known.
There are hundreds of thousands of millions of such Vidyadharas, powerful and prosperous.

In the city of Laṅkā, O Lord, after a long time had passed, some gave their own kingdom to their sons through the traditional succession and went forth; others, by their own power, attained the state of divinity and the bliss of liberation. (PaumaCariya 267–268)

Thus, among those destined for liberation, a son of Meghaprabha named Kīrtidhavala was born from the womb of Padmā, a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) endowed with various virtues and the sovereignty of command, living together with the Vidyādharas. (PaumaCa.
In the city of Laṅkā, he exercises sovereignty at will, like the lord of the gods. (PaumaCa.
270) Thus, by the power of austerity performed over many births, they attain great happiness among gods and humans;
here, having burnt away the remaining defilements and delusion, they become perfected ones (siddhas), stainless and freed from the impurities of karma. (PaumaCa. 271)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Lineage of the Rākṣasas," in the Paumacariya.
[The Chapter on the Ordination and Life of the Rākṣasas and Vānaras:
[The Lineage of the Vānaras: This lineage of the Rākṣasas has been related to you by me in brief.
Listen now, O King, to the origin of the lineage of the monkeys!
On the Vaitāḍhya, the lord of mountains, in the city of Meghapura on the southern range, there was a renowned Vidyādhara chieftain named Ahaṃinda. (PaumaCa. 1–2)

And his wife was Śrīmatī; from her womb was born a son named Śrīkaṇṭha, who possessed great virtues and a splendor like that of a young god. There was also a daughter named Devī, the sister of Śrīkaṇṭha, who had large eyes. (PaumaCārita 3)
In the entire world of living beings, women are like banners of beauty. (PaumaCa.
4) Now, there was a great king named Puṣpottara, a hero who was the lord of the city of Ratnapura; he had a son named Padmottara, who was his equal in virtues. (PaumaCa. 5)
Śrīkaṇṭha’s own sister, Puṣpottarā, sought him for the sake of his learning, yet he did not give her to him; she was given to Kīrtidhavala.
Their marriage was indeed brought about by the great ocean through the decree of fate.
Having heard that for that reason, King Puṣpottara became enraged. (PaumaCa.
7) Then, on another occasion, Śrīkaṇṭha, having gone to Devagiri for worship and returning, saw Kanna in the excellent garden. (PaumaCa. 8)
To her as well, that prince appeared like the god of love in form; at that very moment, a mutual passion arose in both.
Having perceived her state of mind, his body was covered with horripilation due to the force of joy.
Having embraced his ear, King Puṣpottara swiftly flew up into the sky.
Clad in armor and with his mail fastened, the Ceti queen, following her son’s path, rushed after him along the way. (PaumaCariya 10.11)
Skilled in many sciences and statesmanship, Sirikaṇṭha, having understood the ultimate truth, entered the city of Laṅkā as a refuge for the one white with fame.
He was addressed with affection by the Lord of the Rākṣasas, whose mind was delighted.
And he related everything that had occurred as it happened, including the abduction of the maiden.
(PaumaCārita 13) [Vānara-vamśa] [p. 58]

Just then, in the sky, he beheld in the northern direction a vast army approaching— a tumultuous clash of excellent elephants, chariots, infantry, and horses. (PaumaCariya 14) A messenger was dispatched by Kīrtidhavala with words that were both sweet and conciliatory.
Then he too, swift as a bird, quickly reached Puṣpottara.
Having offered a prostration with his head, the messenger spoke to him with sweet words: "O Lord, one who is white with fame has been dispatched to your presence. (PaumaCa. 15–16)
And Prince Śrīkaṇṭha was endowed with an excellent lineage and beauty. (PaumaCa.
18) In this world, the union of supreme beings occurs with those who are supreme; for the lowly and the middling, it is either similar or occurs with their equals. (PaumaCa. 19)
Even when well-guarded and protected with great effort by constant lamentations,
a noble maiden will become an object of others' desire, like the prosperity of a wicked person.
Both belong to the highest lineage, and both possess the beauty of youth and noble character.
"O Lord of Men, let there be a union between these two without obstacle! O Master, there is no need for a battle that causes the slaughter of many people;
indeed, serving the houses of others is the very nature of women. (Padma-Carita 21–22)

While things were proceeding in this very manner, a female messenger arrived and, having prostrated at his lotus-feet, spoke to the Vidyādhara prince. Then Padmā requested him: "O Lord, [I have come] to perform the salutation of your feet."
"O Lord of Men! Sirikaṇṭha has committed no offense at all.
He was seized by me personally; this release of the man is my own rule, arising from the conjunction of the fruition of his karma. (PaumaCa. 24–25)

The king, skilled in many sciences and statesmanship, having reflected in his heart, gave him his daughter and set out quickly for his own city. On a day in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, under an auspicious constellation. (PaumaCa. 26)
The marriage ceremony was performed, unlike any other, for Vasumatī.
Then Kīrtidhavala, bound by intense affection, spoke to Śrīkaṇṭha: PaumaCa.27 [p. 59]
"Do not go to Veyaddha; there are many enemies there for you.
Here, in the salt ocean, there is an island shimmering with the rays of jewels and gems, covered with groves of trees resembling wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees. (PaumaCa. 28–29)
Having previously requested [permission] from the best of gods, Bhīma, Abhīma, and Heḍa—those bulls among the *khēyara*s—came here to this island.
This island has Saṃjhāvēla, Maṇapalhāya, Suvēla, and Kaṇayahari. (PaumaCa. 30)
Nāma, Suōvaṇa, Jalaajjhāya, and Haṃsa;
by name Addhasagga, Ukkaḍaviyaḍa, Amala, Kanta, Phurantarayaṇa, Tōyavalīsa, and Alaca. (PaumaCa. 31–32)
The Dīva, Nabha, Bhānu, Khema, and others such as these are eternally delightful to the mind; they are situated near the Devaramaṇīya [ocean].
In the midst of the salt ocean, there is an island named Vānaradvīpa.
There, together with your kinsmen, you should dwell at ease after building a city enriched with great virtues, emulating the splendor of the foremost gods. (PaumaCa. 34–35)
On the first day of the month of Caitra, Sirikaṇṭha, accompanied by his retinue and fully equipped with chariots, elephants, and horses, flew up toward the island.
He beheld the great ocean, with its waters agitated by surging waves. (PaumaCa. 36)

Having reached the island—which was a vast expanse of sky-like space, a dwelling place for thousands of birds, and enriched with an abundance of excellent jewels—Śrīkaṇṭha descended and settled upon the jeweled rocks there. (PaumaCa. 37–38)
The island appears multicolored due to the radiance of diamonds, sapphires, emeralds, moonstones, and rubies, as if it were garlanded by rays of light;
likewise, it is adorned with five-colored flowers produced from various kinds of young trees. (Pauma-Cariu 39)
It is known by its bees, and by its waterfalls and various mountain caves. (PaumaCa.
