In the meantime, he who had been appointed as a World-Protector (Lokapāla) by Indra— PaumaCa. 37 [p. 131]—[arrived].
Named Nalakubbara, he dwells in Dullabhapura.
Having learned that Rāvaṇa had retreated to Mount Aṭṭhāvaya, King Nalakubbara, filled with rage, dispatched a messenger to him. (PaumaCa. 38–39)
The messenger himself arrived; he was seen in the midst of the assembly by the Lord of Laṅkā, and having been made to pay homage with his head, he sat upon a seat and said:
"O King, this messenger has been dispatched to your presence by Nalakūbara."
He said, "Look here, this city is difficult to overcome, like the peak of Mount Meru.
And he was told by Rāvaṇa: "Until I have gone to the Nandana grove for the purpose of worshipping the Jina temples and return quickly. (PaumaCa. 41–42)
"Stay there with confidence, sporting among beautiful women; O messenger!
Go and speak thus to the Lord of the city that is so difficult to overcome.
Having gone to his master, the messenger, whose speed was as charming as that of thought or the wind, [reported this]. (PaumaCariya 43)
Rāvaṇa related everything that had been said by him in clear meaning. (PaumaCa.
44) Then he constructed a rampart a hundred yojanas wide, filled with fire, along with various kinds of machines designed to destroy the lives of the enemy warriors. (PaumaCa. 45)
Having gone to the Nandana grove and having paid homage to the shrines with devotion,
the ten-faced one returned once more to his own abode.
(PaumaCariya 46) The warriors, led by Prahasta, were fully equipped, their armor fastened, and accompanied by a complete army.
Having reached the city for the sake of seizing it, the Ten-Necked One saw that city, which was difficult to scale, with its high ramparts of fire on all sides;
it was exceedingly hard for vehicles to cross and inspired terror in the enemy warriors. (PaumaCa. 47–48)
"Alas! Even though they are capable, the Rākṣasa Kaucchaḥas, closely allied [with us], are being struck down by our enemy through the employment of many kinds of magical spells.
Then, as those Rākṣasa warriors were being slain, a man was dispatched.
Having approached his master, he said: "O Lord, listen to me!
Those who approach are being burned by the fire crackling on all sides;
those who have attained lordship are being killed in machines with terrifying faces. (PaumaCa. 50–51)
Having heard these words, the ministers of the Lord of Laṅkā, bold in their own intelligence, began to devise a stratagem for the purpose of protecting their own forces. (PaumaCariu 52)

Meanwhile, a female messenger was dispatched by Uparambhā, the wife of Nalakūbara, and she arrived, having been sent by her who was deeply devoted to the affection of the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa). (PaumaCariya 53, p.
Having offered a prostration with his head, the messenger said to Rāvaṇa from one side:
"O Lord, listen to the reason for which you have sent me.
There is a famous woman named Uparañbhā, the wife of Nalakūbara."
Although dismissed by her, I am indeed named Cittamālā.
My heart is eager for a sight of you; bound by love and deeply devoted to your virtues, I think: "Grant me the favor of a vision. (PaumaCa. 55–56)
Pressing both ears [to listen], the son of Ratnashrava spoke thus:
"O beloved, I do not see even a single woman in disguise who is truly beautiful;
for it is contrary to this world and the next that one should ever avoid the wives of others. (PaumaCa. 57)
Even one who eats the remnants of others' food must be a man endowed with firm virtue. (PaumaCa.
58) Having understood the purpose of the messenger, the ministers skilled in that matter said there:
"Even a falsehood must be spoken by those who consider their own welfare. (PaumaCa. 59)
"Sometimes a woman, being pleased, O Lord, might cause a rift in the city; she who has been granted the favor of honor becomes devoted to [the interests of] her suitor.
Having spoken thus, the female messenger was dismissed by the Ten-faced One.
Having gone to her mistress, she related the entire message. (PaumaCa.
61) And having heard the words of the messenger, Upalambhā departed in haste and reached the palace of Daśānana; there she entered and sat down comfortably. (PaumaCa. 62)
And Daśamukha said: "My lady, what pleasure in love-making is there here in the forest?
And it cannot be endured without abandoning Laṅkāpura.
That city was Mayaṇāura, and his science was Āsāliyā.
Having acquired that science, the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), accompanied by his entire host of forces, went to the fortress of Dullaṅghapura and seized its rampart. (PaumaCa. 64–65)
Having heard that Rāvaṇa had arrived and that the rampart had been destroyed,
the king, out of pride, the artisan, suddenly went forth. Then he engaged in battle with the Rākṣasas in the conflict at that very moment.
Amidst a mass of arrows, spears, javelins, and lances being hurled from both sides, the Lord of Laṅkā said: "O blessed lady, you are my teacher; I am at your mercy! (PaumaCa. 67, p. 133)
"Go to the land of Balasamiddha, to the science named Āsāliya.
Born into a noble family, you shall become the wife of Sundara; though conceived in the womb of Kāśadhvaja, remain one who guards her virtue. (PaumaCa. 69–70)
"Even now your beloved lives, O blessed one! Possessing beauty and charm, enjoy distinguished pleasures with him for a long time.
Having thus honored him, King Nalakūbara was released by the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa).
Not perceiving the distinction between faults, he enjoyed pleasures equally with her.
[The battle of Rāvaṇa with Indra:
Having conquered the lord of the city difficult to overcome in the midst of battle, together with his army...
The ten-faced one reached Mount Veyaddha in the realm of Indra.
Having heard there that Rāvaṇa had arrived nearby, Indra asked his father Sahasrāra about the commencement of the seasonal rites. (PaumaCa. 73–74)
Then Sahasrāra said: "My son, this man is endowed with great power and possesses a thousand sciences; it is better to form an alliance with him.
Whether he be equal, superior, or inferior to you, let it be like the union of two measures of grain. (PaumaCa. 75)
Having ascertained the situation, one should then make peace.
It has been said by the ancestors that a conflict with those who are powerful should not be undertaken;
for such a dispute leads to great loss and does not accomplish the objective. (PaumaCariu 76–77)
"Knowing this very thing, my son! Do not be deluded regarding your own duty;
give him your daughter if you desire the kingdom for yourself. (PaumaCā.
77) Having heard these words, Indra’s body was pervaded by intense rage.
Then he began to speak, as if splitting the sky with his voice:
"O Father, how could you utter such piteous words regarding the giving of a daughter to one condemned to death?
Such an act does not befit those who are great in their pride and high status. (PaumaCa. 79–80)

"Even death in battle is praised for noble men of steadfast hearts; even sovereignty, which requires bowing to others, brings about nirvāṇa. Having spoken thus, Śakra quickly entered the armory pavilion.
I set out with diligence, together with the guardians of the world; another chariot followed, adorned with raised flagstaffs and banners.
(PaumaCa.
One [warrior] seizes the *calantacamara* (the waving yak-tail whisk), while another leaps upon the horse that is prancing restlessly.
One calls out for armor and protection for the head; another quickly urges on the clamor of mutual combat with bows, spears, swords, and maces. (Padma Carita 83–84)

Having prepared himself, Indra, together with the circle of world-protectors, mounted Airāvaṇa and departed from his own city, accompanied by the deep sounds of drums, kettledrums, bherīs, kāhalas, and excellent conchs. (PaumaCa. 85)
Having assembled, they began the battle, with the tumultuous sound of trumpets. Hearing the noise of the trumpets, the Rākṣasa army also became greatly agitated;
horses, elephants, chariots, cavalry, and infantry all prepared for combat, prepared for combat.
In that very instant, he equipped everything with weapons and armor—spears, arrows, discuses, lances, swords, and maces—and made it entirely skilled for battle;
there was the sound of various struck musical instruments, and the cavalry and foot soldiers were moving restlessly. (PaumaCārita 88)
The great army of the Rākṣasas was assailed by the soldiers of Indra.

Then, by the warriors of the Lord of the Gods, using iron clubs, spears, javelins, and maces, the vanguard of the Rākṣasa host was broken, with its elephants and horses fleeing in disarray. (PaumaCa. 89–90)
Seeing their own army being crushed by the heroic warriors in battle,
the Rākṣasas, equipped with all their weapons, rushed to their rescue. Vajra, Vajravega, Hastaprahasta, and likewise Mārīci— *Padma-Carita 91*

The warriors Sura, Sāraṇa, Jaḍhara, Gayana, Ujjalama, and others—equipped with armor and fastened with breastplates, their pride and majesty blazing with fierce anger—engaged in battle in such a manner that even Indrabala was forced to retreat. (PaumaCa. 92–93)
Seeing the army led by Śreṇika being broken by the Rākṣasas in battle,
even the soldiers of Indra rose up with joy and vigor.
There were Ghanamālin, Taḍipiṅga, Jvalitākṣa, and Addipaṃjara.
These leaders of the Jalaharas fight together with the Nisācaras. (PaumaCā.
95) Seeing his army of horses, chariots, and infantry destroyed, Mahendra’s son, Prasannakīrti—fierce in battle—rushed forth suddenly, incited by his kinsmen. (PaumaCā. 96)
Then Mālavantaputta, Sirimālin, discharging lotuses, entered the army of the gods like a blazing forest fire in the jungle. (PaumaCa.

"Come, my lord! Be at ease; while I rend him in the forefront of battle with my claws, what need is there for an axe in that which is being torn apart? Thus did a terrible and great battle break out between Śrīmālin and Jayanta. (PaumaCariya 101)
Having drawn his bow with joy, which was crowded with various weapons and from which masses of sparks were rising, Śrīmālī struck Jayanta with an arrow;

Having challenged him in battle, Jayanta, filled with supreme rage, struck Śrīmālin on the middle of his chest; yet, despite that blow, Śrīmālin remained firm.
Seeing him lifeless in the midst of the fray, Indrajit [attacked] Śrīmālin. *Padma-Carita 10.4*
Having driven back the excellent chariot, he turned toward Jayanta.
In the battle, the son of Rāvaṇa pierced the son of the Lord of the Gods with arrows; his body reddened with blood, he fell like a mountain smeared with red ochre. (PaumaCariya 105–106)
Seeing his son Jayanta covered in a profusion of blood from the bees, Indra,
mounted upon Airāvata,
suddenly raised a great clamor with the sound of kettledrums, accompanied by a vast array of elephants, chariots, horses, and infantry.
He surrounded Indrasena on all sides, and [Indra] surrounded Indrakaumāra.
Having observed his son being hemmed in by the divine host in battle, the Lord of Laṅkā, seated upon his excellent chariot, set out toward Indra. (PaumaCariya 108–109)
Indra’s world-protectors, the Āvaḍiyas, and the Rākṣasas, heroes in battle,
discharged a rain of arrows at one another with fierce resentment, using swords,
golden discs, spears, mallets, scimitars, javelins, and spikes. (PaumaCariya 110)
The warriors strike one another, leaving no space between them in battle.

In some places the cries of "Kill! Kill! Kill! are heard; in other places swords clash with the sound "khana khana khana"; and in yet other places there is the sound "taḍa taḍa taḍa" from those whose bodies are pierced by arrows. (PaumaCariya 111–112)
The elephant with the elephants, the excellent chariot with the chariots,
the horse with the horses, and the foot-soldier with the infantry.
(PaumaCariya 113)
Seizing their swords one by one, their prowess attained through the honor of their masters, the heroes of battle fight; the cowardly men flee.
As they fight with joy, the fire of the blows from weapons hurled at one another [rages].
It blazes forth from every side, producing intense heat for the warriors. (PaumaCa.

115) Due to the sound of kettledrums, war-drums, trumpets, the trumpeting of elephants, and the neighing of horses, they cannot hear one another’s voices, even those falling directly into their ears. (PaumaCa. 116)
Struck by swords, arrows, spears,
and javelins, some roll about on the surface of the earth, while others, excellent warriors, rise up and wander about,
their limbs smeared with blood from heads severed and fallen at that very moment. (Pauma-Cariya 117)
In the clamor of the drums of the fierce battle, throngs of headless trunks danced.
Amidst such a combat, where multitudes of hosts of warriors were falling, the charioteer Sumati was then addressed by the Lord of Laṅkā. (PaumaCārita 118–119)
"Drive my excellent chariot swiftly toward Indra in battle;
what is achieved by slaying others of incomparable prowess? For it is this [Indra] who has undertaken the lordship of the gods, which is peerless in virtue and beauty. (PaumaCa. 120)
"I shall destroy all this produced by the power of your science," [he said].
Upon these words, the charioteer quickly drove the chariot—adorned with beautiful banners and possessing a speed like that of thought or the wind—toward Indra. (PaumaCa. 121–122)
Seeing Rāvaṇa approaching, those brave warriors, overcome with fear, began to flee, leaping over one another. Seeing his army broken, Indra, mounted upon Airāvaṇa, became enraged. (PaumaCariya 123)
Discharging a rain of arrows, he drew near to the one named Rākṣasa.
Rāvaṇa, too, with his hands as swift as lightning, quickly split that incoming rain of arrows into two with the strikes of his own shafts. (PaumaCariya 124–125)
Then, filled with rage, the Lord of the Gods took up a weapon of fire and hurled it, blazing like a flame, upon the Lord of Laṅkā.
It was capable of crushing everything and was terrifying to the hosts of Rākṣasas due to its thick heat and smoke. (PaumaCariu 126)
Then Rāvaṇa quickly extinguished it with the Vāruṇa weapon.
But Indra again swiftly discharged the great Tāmasa weapon; Rāvaṇa also quickly destroyed that with the Uddyotana weapon. (PaumaCariu 12.7–8)
Resembling the staff of Yama, these fire-arrows, blazing with the jewels upon their hoods, were released by the Lord of Laṅkā; they bound the entire army of the gods. (PaumaCārita 129)

Seeing his own army bound by the Nāgas and deprived of its joyful defense, the Lord of the Gods, Garuḍa, destroys the serpent-nooses. Seeing him, the Lord of Laṅkā, freed from the serpent-nooses, [the Lord of the Gods]... [PaumaCa. 130]

At that very moment, Śakra also mounted Airāvaṇa, the lord of elephants, who was like a mountain and the sole ornament of the world. Then the ten-faced Rāvaṇa fought with him; indeed, elephant met elephant in battle. (PaumaCa. 131–132)
Both great elephants, possessing the formidable power of their hard tusks and having high maces for teeth, were like two uprooted mountains;
both struck at each other’s blows—with tusks, trunks, and the limbs of men. (PaumaCariya 133)
They trumpet and roar like clouds in the rainy season;
with rut-fluid trickling down, surrounded by the humming of bees, and with their trunks moving restlessly and fiercely, the great elephants fight in battle. (PaumaCa. 134–135)
While the elephants were still fighting, the Lord of the Gods (Indra) was spotted and seized by the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), who slaughtered the elephant-riders;
he was bound with celestial cloth and quickly made to mount his own lordly elephant. (Padma-Carita 13.6)

Free from the pride of his challenge, like the moon released from the grasp of Rāhu, the son of Indra was captured and then released again in the battle with Indrajit. Or rather, what is done with husks once the essence of the grain has been gathered? (PaumaCariu 13.7–8)

From here, the entire army of Indra—including the excellent elephants, horses, and foot soldiers—was routed and fled, reaching the Veyaddha mountain. Having seized [the enemy], the Lord of the Gods, Daśānana, returned accompanied by his own complete host. (PaumaCariya 139)
Setting out toward Laṅkā, he cast a vast shadow over the sky.
Seeing him nearby, the people of the city of Laṅkā and his own retinue came forward to meet him and greeted him with hundreds of auspicious blessings. (PaumaCa. 140–141)
With his parasol raised and a pair of beautiful, shimmering chowries waving, he entered the city of Laṅkā like the Lord of Devas entering the abode of the gods.
Having reached his own palace, which was ablaze with the radiance of various kinds of jewels, PaumaCa. 142.
Amidst the loud-uttered shouts of victory, he descended from his flower-palace.

Having conquered his enemies with armor fastened and donned, and having brought many excellent kings under his command, the Lord of Laṅkā rejoices there, deeply immersed in happiness, through the pure and auspicious merit accumulated in former lives. (PaumaCariya 143–144)
In this *Paumacariya*, the twelfth chapter, titled "The Journey to Veyaddha, the Binding of Indrajit, and the Entry into Laṅkā," is completed.

Then Indra’s warriors, having placed Sahasrāra at their head, reached Rāvaṇa’s palace; announced by the gatekeeper, they were seen. (PaumaCa. 1)

then Sahasrāra spoke to the Ten-faced one with great respect:

"Do not undertake any task while this Indra is obstructed.

"Having swept and smeared this city,
it should be honored with flowers— divine, fragrant, and sweet-smelling.
O Noble One, if you will perform such a service for me starting from today," (PaumaCariya 5).
"I shall release you, O Indra; how else could there be another means? (PaumaCa.
6) Then, at the request of Rāvaṇa, Sahasrāra, together with the world-protectors, agreed to the release of Indra, saying, "If he so desires, all this shall be done. (PaumaCa. 7)
Released by the Lord of Laṅkā, Indra was honored with the majesty of a boon and told: "O noble one, you are my brother.
Enjoy the Veyaddha mountain, residing in the city of Rathanūpura-cakkavāla. (PaumaCa. 8)
"Experience happiness that is delightful to the senses according to your desire.
Having spoken thus, Sahassāra, the lord of the gods, accompanied by the world-protectors, arrived at the city of Rathanūpuracakravāla. (PaumaCa. 9–10)
Having entered his own palace, Śakra was praised by the *vidyādharas*;
the other world-protectors (*lokapālas*) also returned to their respective cities with their retinues. [The dispassion of Indra—] *Padma-Carita* 11.11.

Indra, with an anxious mind, found no steadiness in his palace or on his throne, nor in the excellent flower gardens, nor even in the delightful lotus ponds. [Padma-Carita 12] Indra, overcome by anxiety, did not set his heart upon his consorts; he went to the temple of the Jina.
Having gone there and paid homage to him, he desired to break [the bow], reflecting:
"Alas! Oh, what a misfortune! What can be done with the supernatural power of the *khēyara*s, which is as flickering as lightning and resembles a streak of Indra’s bow? (PaumaCa. 13–14)
Those very sciences, those warriors, and those elephants and horses—along with the strength of one's arms—all become like mere grass at the conclusion of one's merit. (Padma Carita 15, p.
Out of compassion for me, the Lord of Laṅkā became my supreme kinsman; though he was attached to worldly pleasures, he has awakened me here. (PaumaCā.
16) Having abandoned all pleasant associations that delight the senses and the mind...
"I shall take up the renunciation that destroys evil, according to the doctrine of the Supreme Jina.
At that very place, the sage named Nivāṇasaṅgama descended from the path of the sky into that temple of the Jina. (PaumaCa. 17–18)
Having seen the lord of sages, he himself rose up with great joy; bowing his head, he paid homage with the highest devotion. (PaumaCa.
19) The ascetic, too, having performed the proper conduct toward the images of the moon-like lords of Jinas...
Seated upon the offered seat, shining with the glory of his ascetic splendor, the sage was addressed once more by Śakra with supreme reverence.
[The account of Indra’s previous birth—
] Having bowed again, Śakra questioned the sage with the utmost humility.
"Master! Tell me my previous birth exactly as it occurred. (PaumaCa. 21) Then the ascetic began to relate that connection with his former life:
"While wandering about in some way, you indeed obtained a human birth. (PaumaCa. 22)
In the city named Sihipura, there was a family of oil-pressers; in that family, a daughter was born who lacked auspicious marks and qualities, her body afflicted by various diseases.
Both her mother and father passed away due to the force of their karma. (Pauma-Cariya 23)
With great difficulty she sustained her life on food that was loathsome to the world. (PaumaCa.
24) With her hands and feet cracked, her body emaciated, and wearing tattered rags, she wandered about with a sorrowful mind, being mocked by the people. (PaumaCa. 25)

Through the exhaustion of her karma, having passed away there, she was reborn as a female *kiṃpuruṣa* named Kṣīradhārā (Milk-stream). Having fallen from that state, she entered the womb of Dhāriṇī in the city of Ratnapura.
The son of the merchant Gomukha, Sahasrabhāga, attained right conviction (*samyaktva*);
endowed with the minor vows (*anuvrata*), he passed away and was reborn in the Śukra celestial mansion. (PaumaCa. 27–28)
Having descended from the celestial chariot, he was born as the son of Guṇavallī in the city of Pūrvila-ralasañcaya, and indeed in the city of Maṇirata. (PaumaCa.
Then Nandivardhana, having ruled the kingdom, went forth into the homeless life together with the Best of Jinas;
having practiced austerities, he attained the highest status in the Graiveyaka heavens.
Having enjoyed the supreme bliss of an Indra there, he passed away and was reborn here in the land of Bharata.
Born as Maṇasundara, you became Indra, the son of Sahasrāra.
Having attained the status of Indra, through a mental aspiration during the time of your conception here in the city of Cakravāla, you were born as the sovereign of the Vidyādharas. (PaumaCa. 31–32)
"Why do you grieve so long? I have not been defeated in battle.
By this very cause, you shall be liberated from the stain of karma.
Do you not remember what was done previously by me, while playing, even though I was difficult to overcome? (PaumaCariya 33)
I shall tell you all that regarding the earth and water; listen with a one-pointed mind. (Pauma-Cariu 34) In the city of Ariñjayapura, there was a lord of the khecara-s named Jvalanaśikha;
his wife was Vegavatī, and their daughter was Āhallā. (Pauma-Cariu 35)
At her svayaṃvara, many various kinds of vidyādharas assembled with an abundance of power and supernatural success; you too arrived at that very place. (PaumaCa.
36) [The lord of the excellent city of Candrāvatta was named Ānandamālin.]
He was chosen at her *svayaṃvara* by the power of karma from a previous existence.
Having married that maiden, who was perfect in beauty and youth, the lord of men, immersed in an ocean of passion, enjoyed pleasures like a supreme god. (PaumaCa. 37–38)
From that time on, O Lord, your body was overcome with anger at the sight of Īśāna,
yet you did not abandon your pursuit of him, Nandīmālin. Then, on another occasion, he was awakened by the exertion of his ascetic practice.
Nandimālin went forth, having abandoned possessions and worldly undertakings.
Wandering as a great-souled ascetic accompanied by other monks, he reached the bank of the river Haṃsāvalī and was seen by you as you were roaming about. (PaumaCa. 40–41)
And the monk was observed by you while absorbed in meditation on Mount Rahāvatta;
whatever happened regarding that river, all the causes of the commotion were seen by you.
Angrily, you bound the ascetic with ropes on all his limbs. (PaumaCa. 42)

Nevertheless, the ascetic does not tremble, like Mount Meru before the gusts of wind. Seeing the ascetic, the virtuous monk named Kallāṇaguṇadhara, who was his own brother, [the king] became enraged and subjected him to an assault while he was in the meditative posture (paḍimā). (PaumaCa. 43–44)
Having quickly burned him with the fire of his wrath and then having investigated thoroughly, the Great Sage was pacified by your wife, who possessed all splendor. (PaumaCa.
Seeing that woman, the ascetic, whose mind was cultivated in rightness, became filled with compassion and his heart was instantly purified. (PaumaCa.
46) He who reviles an ascetic of firm conduct, who is free from possessiveness and egoism—
The fool strikes and laments; he attains a long cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
Having understood this distinction between merit and demerit, you should know that only through Dharma is this abode of suffering severed. (PaumaCa. 47–48)
Having heard his own life story, Śakra, filled with genuine spiritual emotion (*saṃvega*), bowed again and again to the seated sage who had realized the ultimate truth;
then, having given him instruction, the sage departed for his own place. (PaumaCa. 49)
Indra installs his son Viryadatta upon the entire kingdom.
Having taken leave of his mother, father, kinsmen, and wives, Śakra, the Jina, undertakes the ascetic life for the sake of liberation from suffering. (PaumaCariya 50–51)
By means of the practice of austerity through the offering of food to one another, having brought about the destruction of the impurity of karma,
and having attained a state of stainless purity through the arising of knowledge, Indra reached the auspicious state (nirvāṇa), his purpose fully accomplished.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Nirvāṇa by Indra," in the *Paumacariya*.
[The Section on the Teaching of Anantavīrya] Now that lord of the gods, having gone to Mount Meru, [visited] the shrines...
Having observed [the situation], he turned back and returned with his characteristic grace.
Hearing a sound like the deep rumble of thick clouds, Rāvaṇa was agitated;
looking about, he saw the circle of the quarters colored with saffron.
Mārīci asked: "Whose is this sound, like the roar of clouds?
Or what is this that has rendered the world with the hue of twilight?
Then Mārīci said: "Upon the Golden Peak (Suvaṇṇatuṅga) of Anantavīrya..."
The omniscient knowledge (kevala-jñāna), which illuminates both the worlds and that which is beyond them, has arisen.

For living beings, this is rooted in the presence of the virtuous; for the gods, it is this sound of celestial drums, by the dust spread from the rays of their jeweled crowns, the entire world is overspread. (Pauma-Cariya 4–5)
Having heard his words, Rāvaṇa descended, filled with joy; he paid homage to the bull among the best of sages, having performed three circumambulations. (PaumaCa. 6)
Having first paid homage to him, the gods sat down; then the second [to enter] was like the lord of the gods (Indra), and there also sat the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa).
Then, among the gods and humans, and among the lords of the sky-dwellers (khecaras) who were seated on their thrones...
There, the ascetic Śīsa was asked about the Dharma that is beneficial for living beings.

That lifespan of the first Kulagara was thus proclaimed by the Jinas. (PaumaCa.
99) In this way, for each successive tenth part, the portion of the lifespan-decad diminishes for the remaining Kulagars; and for Nābhi, it is ten million years. (PaumaCa. 100)

The lifespan of Ṛṣabha was eighty-four hundred thousand *pūrvas*; that of Ajita was seventy-two; for the next six, there is a decrease of ten [thousand] each. For the two Jinas [after them], the *pūrva* lifespans are, in order, two hundred thousand and one hundred thousand.

Eighty-four, seventy-two, sixty, thirty, ten, and one—these are the lakhs of years for the six supreme Jinas; furthermore, fifty-nine thousand, eighty-four [thousand], and [another] should be known. (PaumaCa. 102–103)
Fifty-five, thirty-five, ten thousand, one thousand, and one hundred years;
from here, there are seventy-two years [between the Jinas].
(PaumaCa. 104) [In the interval between the Jinas, there are twelve Cakravartins; their former births and so forth—]
Thus, O Śreṇika, the lifespan of the Tīrthaṅkaras has been explained by me;
now hear from me which Cakravartin appeared in the interval between each.
In the case of Ṛṣabha, Bharata was born of Sumaṅgalā as the first Cakravartin.
In a previous birth, he was the arm of Puṇḍarīkiṇī;
as the son of the Jina Vajrasena, having died, he attained Sarvārtha. Then, having passed away from there and become Bharata, he went to liberation. (PaumaCa. 106–107)
In the city of Puhai, King Vijaya, having obtained the venerable Yaśodhara as his preceptor,
went forth into the religious life and ascended to the excellent celestial vehicle (vimāna) named Vijaya.
Having passed away from Kośalā, he was born as Vijaya by Yaśavatī.
Sagara, through the separation from his sons, practiced austerity and went to liberation. (PaumaCa.
109) Then, in Puṇḍarīgiṇī, Sasiprabha, having received the Jina-initiation at the feet of the stainless supreme sage Vimala, became an excellent god in the Graiveyaka heaven. (PaumaCa. 110)
Then, having descended from there, he was born as Maghavan, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), to King Sumitra and Queen Bhāminī in Śrāvastī.
Between the Jinas Dharma and Śānti, he enjoyed the realm of Bharata.
Having practiced the austerity of the best of Jinas, he went to the Sanatkumāra kalpa. (PaumaCa.
112) [The Life Story of the Cakravartin Sanatkumāra]
Then Saṇaṅkumāra, of exquisite form and renowned throughout the three worlds, was born as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), a steadfast one during that very interval between Jinas.
Then the King of Magadha asked: "By what power of merit was this produced?"
“Let him come, for he is of beautiful form; tell me the secret, O Blessed One!
“In brief, the Gaṇadhara tells the entire connection of the Purāṇas:
‘In this land of Bharata, there is a village named Govardhana. (PaumaCa. 115)

There lived a householder named Jinadatta, born of a noble family, who, having practiced constant austerity, passed away and attained a happy rebirth. Due to his separation from him, his wife Vinayavatī [constructed] a very large temple for the Jina. (PaumaCa. 116)
Having had [this] performed with a firm mind, I took up the life of renunciation. There dwelt a householder named Meghabāhu;
he was auspicious, possessed of right view, steadfast, and full of energy. (PaumaCa. 117–118)
Having seen the great worship performed at the temple of the Jina by Vinayamati, Mātaṅga placed his faith in it;
thereupon he was reborn as a yakṣa, and he performs service for the fourfold community of śramaṇas. (PaumaCariu 119)

Devoted to the teaching of the Jina and possessing a firm disposition of pure right conviction, he, upon falling from that state, was born as King Dhammarui, the son of Tilayasundarī, the wife of King Suprabha, in the city of Mahāpura. (PaumaCa. 120–121)
The disciple of the venerable Suppaha became endowed with vows, the codes of conduct, and restraints;
free from the faults of suspicion and the like, he was indifferent even toward his own body. With a mind devoted to the Saṅgha, he was diligent in service and great in virtue. (PaumaCa. 122)

Having undergone the law of time (death), he became a supreme god in the Māhendra heaven. (*Padma-Carita* 123) Descending from that celestial chariot of the immortals, he was born as Sanatkumāra, the wheel-turning monarch, to the queen of King Sahadeva in the city of Gayapura. (*Padma-Carita* 124)
Having heard the description of his form alone, which surpasses that of the lords of the Saudharma heaven, two gods fell into doubt; upon seeing him, they descended.
Seeing the universal monarch, the gods exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! PaumaCa. 125.
"Your form is most beautiful, praised even by Śakra.
Then the Cakravartin said: "O gods! If you have come to see me, wait for a single moment; wait until I have bathed and finished my meal. (PaumaCa. 126–127)
Alas! Having performed wicked deeds, his body adorned with all ornaments, the Wheel-turning King was seen by the gods as he sat upon his lion-throne. (PaumaCa. 128)
"From this point on, the gods say: 'This beautiful form of yours is supreme, yet there is only one flaw here: that it is by nature momentary.
For at the very first sight, you possessed a splendor befitting your youth. (Padma-Carita 129)
In an instant, how was her beauty lost by that exceedingly swift force?
Having heard the words of the gods and knowing that human birth is impermanent,
the wheel-turning monarch renounces the world and performs severe ascetic practice.
Having endured his illnesses, endowed with manifold supernatural attainments and great strength, he passed away from there and went to the heaven of Sanatkumāra. (PaumaCa.
132) Now, in Puṇḍarīkiṇī, Meharatha [was the son] of Ghanaratha; he was afflicted by disease...
Having undergone the law of time (death), he became a supreme god in Sarvārtha [heaven].
Having descended from there, he was born as a son in the womb of Queen Viśvasenā in Nāgapura; he is Śānti, the bringer of peace to living beings. (PaumaCariya 133–134)
Having enjoyed the realm of Bharata and established a *tīrtha*, he became the sixteenth of the Jinas and the fifth of the Cakravartins. (PaumaCa.
135) Both Kunthu and Ara were Cakravartins and arose as Tīrthaṅkaras.
Having destroyed the impurity of karma, they attained the auspicious, stainless, and unsurpassed state. (PaumaCa.
136) Between the Jinas Dharma and Śānti, there were three Jinas who were also Cakravartins—namely, Sanatkumāra and the others. This interval is to be understood as follows. (PaumaCa. 137)
In the city of Dhannapura, O Lord of Men! that lord of men, having been a disciple of the sage Vicittagutta, died and attained the world of the gods.
Having descended from that celestial mansion, [he was born] as the son of the wife of the Lord of Sāvatthī. *Padma-Carita* 138.
To Tārā was born a son of Kṛtavīrya named Subhūma (PaumaCa.139). Having slain Paraśurāma, the son of Jamadagni, in battle, he became a Cakravartin, a hero, and a lord of jewels (PaumaCa.140).

Having rendered the earth devoid of brahmins and having lived out his time free from the vow of celibacy, he reached the seventh hell due to his attachment to the accumulation of dense evil. [Padma-Carita 141] There was a king named Cintāmaṇi in the city of Vītasoka.
Having obtained [the state of] Suprabha-guru, he was reborn in the fifth aeon (PaumaCa.
142). Having passed away in Nāgapura, he was born as the son of Mahāpaumā, the queen of King Paumaraha; then he became the wheel-turning monarch Mahāpauma (PaumaCa. 143).
His eight daughters, endowed with the excellence of beauty, did not wish for a husband, as they had been carried off by the lords of the *khēcaras*. (PaumaCariya 144)
Having been summoned and brought there, they all departed after taking their leave;
then, at the time of their passing, they were reborn in the celestial realm. As for those eight men who were the Vidyādhara princes, due to the separation from them— PaumaCa. 145.
Disenchanted, she went forth into the religious life and attained an excellent celestial mansion of the gods. (PaumaCa.

146) The awakened wheel-turning monarch, having conceived a sense of spiritual urgency due to his daughter’s [suffering], gave the kingdom to Padma and went forth into homelessness together with Viṣṇu. (PaumaCa. 147)

The ascetic Mahāpadma, having performed austerities enriched by great virtues, attained the state of an *ṛṣipabbhāra*; the steadfast one [lived] between Ara and Mallī. (PaumaCa. 148) There was a king named Mahindadatta in Vijayapura, possessed of great power.
Having been a disciple of the sage Nandana, he went to the Māhendra heaven. (PaumaCa.
149) Having descended in Kampilla, he was born as Harisena, the son of Vappa, the king of Harikela; he became a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), renowned throughout the world. (PaumaCa. 150)
Having made the entire earth adorned with Jina temples, he went forth as a monk at the holy site of Munisuvrata; freed from karma, he attained liberation. (PaumaCa.
151) King Amiyappabha, in Rājapura, [attained] the status of a disciple of the sage Suhamma.
Having made Brahma-loka his own through the virtues of austerity and self-restraint,
he descended from there and was born as the son of Queen Yaśomatī in Rājapura;
he became the heroic wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) Jayasena, the sovereign of the entire Bhārata.

Having developed a state of spiritual urgency and having taken up the initiation taught by the Jina, he who aimed at the destruction of the eight types of karma attained perfection between the two Jinas Nami and Nemi.
Formerly, in Vārāṇasī, at the feet of the ascetic Tiliṅga... [PaumaCariya 154]
Having been born, he went forth into the religious life and practiced twelvefold asceticism.
Then, after passing away while absorbed in deep meditation, he was born as a preeminent lord of the gods in the Kamalagumma heaven, adorned with earrings and ornaments of exquisite craftsmanship.
There, in that excellent celestial mansion, accompanied by a host of divine nymphs and possessing great majesty,
he enjoys delightful sensual pleasures endowed with supreme qualities. Having descended from that mansion, [he was born] as the wife of King Brahmadatta.

And having been born as Brahmadatta in Kampilla [to the mother] Puṣpacūlā, and having enjoyed the land of Bharata and performed deeds free from passion, he passed away and entered the seventh hell during the interval between the Jinas Nemi and Pārśva. (PaumaCariya 158–159)
"These lords of the earth, O Śreṇika, twelve wheel-turning monarchs (cakravartins) have been described by me; they manifest the fruit of merit before the eyes of people. — *Padma-Carita* 160.
[The Fruit of Merit and Demerit:
That men always dwell happily in palaces as lofty as mountain peaks—that is the fruit of the tree of Dharma; all of this is manifest here in the world. (PaumaCa. 161)
That men dwell in houses adorned with lattices, yet devoid of wealth and grain—that is the fruit of the tree of evil. (PaumaCa.
162) [And likewise] in horses and elephants, adorned with waving chowries and of various kinds...
Whatever kings endure, that is the fruit of the tree of Dharma. (PaumaCa.
163) Those who, exhausted by thirst and hunger, their bodies overcome by cold and heat, walk upon foot—that is all the fruit of the tree of evil. (PaumaCa. 164)

Whatever excellent food kings eat from golden vessels, endowed with eighteen qualities—all that is the fruit of the tree of merit. And food devoid of flavor, served in jars, small pots, or shallow dishes— [is the fruit of demerit]. PaumaCa. 165.1–2.
That which they eat as poor food is the fruit of the tree of evil. (PaumaCa.
166) That they become great beings such as Tīrthaṅkaras, Cakravartins, Baladevas, Vāsudevas, and others, is the fruit of the tree of Dharma. (PaumaCa. 167)
This fruit of merit and demerit has been briefly described; now listen, O Śreṇika, to the births of Balarāmas and Vāsudevas [and their various associated places]. PaumaCa. 168.
Nāgapura, Sāketā, Sāvatthī, and likewise Kōsambī;
Pōyaṇapura, Sīhapura, Sēlapura, and Kōsambī; again Pōyaṇapura—these are the cities of the Vāsudevas. (PaumaCa. 169)
In due course, in his subsequent existence, he experienced all [pleasures] resembling those of the city of the gods. PaumaCa.
170. And the first was Vissabhūī, then Pabayaa, then Dhaṇamitta, Sāgaradatta, Piyamitta, and Laliyamitta. PaumaCa. 171.
Likewise, the one named Puṇarvasu was the ninth; furthermore, in a previous birth, there was the sage Gaṅgadatta. All of these were indeed Keśavas.
In the case of the first, his fall from heaven occurred while he was fighting for the sake of seizing a woman. (PaumaCariya 172)
The pleasure garden and the forest become a place of death, and the sporting in the woods likewise becomes a source of grief.
There is an absolute attachment to sense objects, as well as their separation and supreme deformity. (PaumaCārita 173)
"These were the causes of destiny that existed for Keśin in his previous birth" (PaumaCa. 174).
"Therefore, do not practice asceticism accompanied by a causal motive even for a moment out of delusion;
it increases the cycle of existence and is the root of all sufferings" (PaumaCa. 175).
Saṃbhūta, Saṃbhava, Sudarśana, Śreyāṃsa, Aibhūti, Vasubhūti, and likewise the sage Ghoṣasena;
after these, Udadhi and Drumasena—these were the foremost of sages. (Pauma-Cariu 176)
In a previous existence, they were gurus, in due order, of the Vāsudevas here [in this world].
[They resided in] the Kalpa of Mahāsukka, the Pāṇaya Kalpa, and Ācua;
as well as Sahassāra, Sōdhamma, Māhinda, and Cēva Sōdhamma. (PaumaCa. 177–178)
Kappa, Saṇaṅkumāra, and likewise Mahāsukka by name—having fallen from these [heavens], all these Keśavas were reborn.
[In the cities of] Pōyaṇapura, Vāripura, Mahāpura, and the city named Sānti. PaumaCa. 179.
Cakrapura, Kusāgra, Mithilā, Sāketa, and Mathurā—PaumaCa. 180.
In these cities, the Keśavas, endowed with great strength, were born; hereafter, I shall describe in order the fathers of them all. PaumaCa. 181.
The first was Prabhāpāti, the lord of the land of Brahmā; then Rudranāman, Soma, Śivaṃkara, and also Agnidāna, who was pure and equanimous.
Then there was Daśaratha, the king of men, and Vasudeva, the monarch, in due order. *Padmacarita* 182.
These were the beloved wives of all the Vāsudevas: PaumaCa.
183–184. First was Migāvatī, then Mādhavī, Puhaī, Sīyā, Ambikā, Lacchī, Kēsī, and Kēgaī.
Likewise, Devakī here [is one]; these mothers of the Vāsudevas are indeed their wives. Listen now as I speak of them:
the first is Sayaṃprabhā, then Ruppiṇī, Pabhavā, and Maṇoramā. (PaumaCa. 185)

Having heard this, Vimalasundarī and Nandavatī likewise [were filled with joy]. From that time on, Prabhāvatī and Rūpiṇī—possessing virtue, beauty, and youth—became the chief queens of all the Vāsudevas. (PaumaCariya 186–187)
[The Baladevas and their various associated places: Dhavalagrasanniveśa, the city of Puṇḍarīkiṇī is called the first on earth, Ānandapurī, and Nandapurī is also to be known. (PaumaCa. 188)
The cities were Aśokā, the enchanting Vijayapura, Susīmā, Khemā, and Nāgapura; these were the birthplaces of the Rāmas.
Subala, Pavanavega, Nandi, Sumitra, and Mahābala likewise [were the birthplaces of the Lakṣmaṇas]. (PaumaCariya 189)
And from here, Sudarśana is to be known as Puruṣavṛṣabha;
Śramaṇa is indeed Vasundhara, and Śrīcandra is the last, Saṅkha. (PaumaCa. 190) [p. 196]
These were the names of the Baladeva-munis in their previous births: Anagāra was the first bull among sages; then came the one named Śramaṇasiṃha;
the third was Suvratarṣi; and likewise Vasabha and Prajāpāla. (PaumaCa. 191–192)
Dhamadharo, Sudhammo, Sāyaraghoso, and Vidyanābho—these were his gurus in his previous birth, indeed the upholders of the lineage of the Sīradhāris.
Furthermore, three [of them] came from Anuttara, and three from Sahasrāra. (PaumaCa. 193)
Two descended from the Brahma heaven, while one descended from the tenth heaven.
Having fallen from these [heavens], they were born as the ascetic Baladeva, who was rich in austerity.
O Śreṇika, I shall now tell you about their mothers in this birth. (PaumaCa. 194–195)
Bhadrā named Subhadrā, Sudarśanā, Suprabhā, likewise Vijayā and another, Vējayantī, Śīlā, and Avarājitā; furthermore, after these, Rohiṇī of excellent form is mentioned. *Padmacarita* 196.
These were the mothers here of the Sīradhārin [Tīrthaṅkaras]: Śreyāṃsa and Tiviṭṭha [were sons of] Vaṃdantī, and Keśava [was the son of] Jina;
these five were the lotuses among the best of men. Between the Jinas Ara and Malla, there was Āsā. (PaumaCa. 197–198)
Malli and Munisuvrata are declared to be Datta;
Kesava is said to be among Subvaya and Namī; furthermore, Kesi is Lakṣmaṇa.
Ariṣṭanemi pays homage [to them], as does the last Kesava, endowed with great strength. (PaumaCa. 199)
From here, having traversed seven *ghaṭīs*, I shall go to all the cities—
[the various places belonging to the Prativāsudevas and their associates]: Alakāpurī, Vijayapura, Nandanapura, and Pṛthivīpura.

Furthermore, Haripura, Sūrapura, and the one named Siṃha, as well as the city of Laṅkā and Rājagṛha—these, O Śreṇika, were known in ancient times as the cities of the Prativāsudevas. (PaumaCa. 201–202)
Āsaggīva, Tāraga, Mēraga, and then Mahukēḍa;
there is also the powerful Nisumbha, as well as Palhāa and Rāvaṇa;
and the ninth is Jarāsaṃdha—these are the adversaries of Keśava in due order.
In this land of Bhārata, there were enemies of the Keśins. PaumaCa.
204: The first was Suvarṇakumbha, then Kittidhara, and the one named Sudharman; then Hariṇakuśa, Kittī, Sumitra, and Bhuvanaśobha. PaumaCa. 205.
And the sage Suvrata said: "Siddhārtha is the last of these Baladevas; they were all my teachers in this very birth.
And the eight Baladevas have attained the supreme state of the eternal realm of Śiva."
And one alone appeared as the very last in the Brahma-world.
Thus, having embraced the vast forest of karma with the vine of exertion and burned it all with the great fire of dhyāna, some here have gone to liberation.
In other births, those lives remaining were stained and situated within the cycle of existence; yet through the fruit of the Dharma, they became stainless and forever abodes of happiness.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Lives of the Tīrthaṅkaras and Others," in the *Paumacariya*.
[The Description of the Majesty of the One Possessing the Glory of Many Virtues and Fame] [The Origin of the Harivaṃśa]—
O Sēṇiya! Listen now to the connection concerning the eighth Rama.
I shall tell you the entire account of the origin of your family lineage exactly as it occurred. (PaumaCa.
1) At the time of the Tīrthaṅkara Śītala, there was a king named Sumukha in the city of Kauśāmbī; and in that very place lived a weaver named Vīraya. (PaumaCa. 2)
Having abducted his wife named Vanamālā, King Anaṅga enjoyed there a wealth of pleasures, like the God of Love in the company of Rati. Then,
on another occasion, the lord of men, having given wholesome alms to a sage...
Reborn in Harivarṣa together with his wife, he was tormented by the grief of separation from his beloved.
Having taken up the ascetic life at the feet of the sage Pōṭṭilaka, he passed away and became an excellent god. (PaumaCa. 4–5)
Having recognized [the couple] by means of his supernatural power (*avadhijñāna*), the god swiftly abducted the pair born in Harivarṣa and brought them to the city of Campā.
Because he was born in Harivarṣa and was brought here after being abducted, [he is known as Harivaṃśa].
By that very [lineage], Harirāja became renowned throughout the three worlds (PaumaCa.
7). His son was born as Mahāgiri, endowed with beauty; and in due course, a son named Himagiri was born to him as well (PaumaCa. 8).
Vasugiri and Indragiri were born; likewise, King Ratnamālī became Sambhūta, and from him, Bhūtadeva was born. (PaumaCariu 9, p.
King Mahīdhara and many other such preeminent leaders of men were born in the Harivaṃśa; they have passed away after a long period of time. (PaumaCariya 10) [The Life of Munisuvrata Jina]
In that very same Harivaṃśa lineage, a king named Sumitra was born; he ruled the city of Kusaggapura, and his queen was Paumāvatī.
Once, while she was sleeping comfortably during the last watch of the night— PaumaCa. 11.6a.
Now, while she was sleeping happily in the final watch of the night...
She, being auspicious due to the application of the sacred texts, beheld fourteen dreams:
an elephant, a bull, a lion, an ablution, a garland, the moon, the sun, a banner, a pitcher, a lotus pond, an ocean, a celestial palace, a mountain, a heap of jewels, and a fire. (PaumaCa. 12–13)
The lotus-faced lady awoke and related the fourteen dreams to her husband; he replied to her, "A supreme Jina shall be born as your son.
Even while this conversation was still underway, the sky suddenly began to rain.
And a rain of jewels fell, illuminating the ten directions. (PaumaCa.
15) For fifteen months, the Yakṣa Dhanada rained down three and a half crores of jewels every single day. (PaumaCa. 16)
Then, having descended into a womb adorned by goddesses dwelling in the filaments of lotuses,
that one of meritorious deeds gradually became the Lord of Jinas.
As soon as he was born there, he was led by the gods to the summit of Mount Mandara.
He was bathed by Indra and the other gods with the waters of the Ocean of Milk. Then,
after his consecration had been performed and his body adorned with all ornaments,
Indra and the other preeminent deities praised him with hundreds of auspicious hymns.
Then, having offered their prayers, they departed;
the wise general also, having placed Jinacandra on his mother’s lap, went to the temple, and she too, while he was still in the womb, had been virtuous even as a queen. (PaumaCa. 20)
The name "Muṇisuvrata" was bestowed upon the Jina by his elders.
Gradually he grew up, and after enjoying the kingdom for a long time, he became awakened [to the truth] upon seeing an autumn cloud dissolving away. (PaumaCa. 21–22)
The bull-like Jina Munisuvrata, surrounded by gods, established his son Suvrata on the throne; then the Blessed One, together with kings, became a wandering mendicant.
During the observance of the sixth fast at Rājagṛha, by King Vṛṣabhadatta—
And with supreme food, the fast-breaking meal was given to the Lord of Jinas. And by the power of the Jina, Vṛṣabhadatta attained five hundred sons. (PaumaCa. 24)
With his feet honored by gods and asuras, the Tīrthaṅkara wanders upon the earth. (PaumaCa.
25) Beneath a Campaka tree, as the Blessed One meditated thus through the destruction of the destructive karmas, omniscience (kevalajñāna) arose. (PaumaCa. 26)
Then Subāhu also, having bestowed the kingdom there upon his capable son, became a mendicant,
practiced austerities, passed away, and attained perfection.
Having established the ford (tīrtha), the Lord Munisuvrata also, accompanied by his retinue, [passed away].
On the summit of Mount Sammeta, he attained liberation, which is release from suffering. (PaumaCa.
28) [The Origin of King Janaka:
The first son of Dakṣa was born by the name of Ilavardhana.

The prince was Śrīvardhana, and a son was born to him as well. Śrīvatsa was his son; from him were born Saṃjayanta, the bull among kings, Kuṇima, and Mahāraha. Thus, many kings arose in the Harivaṃśa lineage. (PaumaCa. 29–30)
Some have passed away in due course, some have attained perfection through austerity here,
while others have been reborn in the celestial realm by their own merit. Thus,
when many aeons had elapsed, *Padma-Carita* 31.5.
Born in Mithilā, he was Vāsavaketu of the Harivaṃśa lineage (PaumaCa.
32). His wife was Surūpā, named Ilā, who was preeminent in virtues in the world;
in her womb a son was born named Janaka (PaumaCa. 33).
O Śreṇika, the lineage of Janaka has indeed been told by me in brief; now listen to the dynasty in which King Daśaratha was born. (PaumaCa.
34) [The Origin of King Daśaratha]

The times pass away; those ascetics who are truly diligent undergo penance, while those attached to sense-objects revel and wither away, having failed to perform meritorious deeds. Thus do living beings experience both sufferings and pleasures in this world of the living. (PaumaCariya 35)
For them, calamities and great festivals alike revolve in turn. (PaumaCa.
36) The sages meditate upon dhyāna; those free from passion censure the impassioned. The wise who are sober rejoice, while those addicted to wine and meat become deluded. (PaumaCa. 37)
Those deluded by sense objects sing, and those afflicted by disease weep;
while those who are happy laugh upon seeing people suffering.
Those of a quarrelsome nature dispute, and likewise some wail and run about. (Pauma-Cariya 38)
Some, out of greed and thirst for battle, go to war; in this way, through various means such as days and times, one is drawn away. (PaumaCa.
200] Thus, by various methods, one is led astray over the course of days and time.
Like the fading of a painted image, the downward-ascending age (avasarpinī) wanes.
Then, in the twentieth interval between Jinas occurring from this point, a king named Vijaya became the sovereign of the city of Sāketapura. (PaumaCa. 40–41)
To that Mahādevī Himacūlā, two sons were born: the first was Vajrabāhu, and the second was named Purandara.
(PaumaCariya 42) Furthermore, at that time, King Bahuvāhana resided in Nāgapura.
His wife was Cūḍāmaṇi, and his daughter was Manoharā.
Then Vajrabāhu went and, with great joy, married that maiden who had been given by Aha-vāhana to his eldest son Vijaya. (PaumaCariya 43–44)
When the marriage was being prevented, her brother Udayasundara began to lead that maiden away;
accompanied by him, she went to her father-in-law’s house. (PaumaCa. 45) [The sight of the excellent sage—]
Then, during the spring season, on the summit of Mount Vasantagiri, the lord of sages was seen by Vajrabāhu as he was passing by, absorbed in meditation.
As Vajravara-bāhu drew closer to him on the mountain, [he beheld him]. (PaumaCa. 46)
In that way, their affection increases, like a grove of excellent flowering trees.

With waists so slender they could be grasped by the palms of the hands, and with broad hips, arms, and thighs;

Because of that deed by which Sītā was distressed,
she was sought out by Rāma on the southern side of the Veyaddha range, in the northern direction of Mount Kailāsa.
There are many countries, filled with villages, towns, and cities.
Right there, however, is a single region named Addhababbara,
which is terrible, devoid of self-restraint and virtue, and crowded with many heretics.
There, in the city of Maūramāla, which was crowded with barbarian folk,
lived a king named Āyaraṅga, whose firm strength was like that of Yama.
[In] Kambōja, Suya, Kavōya, and other regions, there were also many barbarian people.
Among these, those who were kings were the sons of Āyaraṅga. [PaumaCa.
7] Now, on a certain occasion, King Babbara invaded the territory of Janaka.
The army of the Cīla people, fully equipped, began to lay waste [the land].

Having gone and paid homage, he related the entire arrival of the Mlecchas and the destruction of the country, as well as that which had been commanded by his father.
"O Lord," he said, "your father, who is affectionate toward his subjects, having offered salutations, makes this request of you: [PadmaCariu 10]
The entire region has been laid waste by great bandits.
O Lord, for this reason there are many laymen and ascetics, and the temples of the Lords of Jinas have been destroyed; come quickly for their protection! (PaumaCa. 11–12)
Having spoken thus, the bull among men summoned Rāma and, with the entire force assembled, began to bestow the kingdom upon him. (PaumaCa.
13) With golden jars in hand, the heroes [proclaimed it] amidst the sound of drums and the chanting of bards.
While Rāma remained steadfast before him for the sake of his sovereignty, Rāghava, seeing such a display, spoke these words:
"O warriors, for what reason have you gathered here with jars in your hands? (PaumaCa. 14–15)
Then Daśaratha said, "O son! The army of the Mlecchas has arrived;

Rāma, with a smiling face, replied, "Father, why [fight] those who are like beasts? (PaumaCa. 16)
"Go upwards, O one of great glory, together with me, your son! Having heard these words, the lord of men, his heart filled with joy, said:

Pauma says:
"O Lord of Men!

Having heard Rama’s words, the king spoke thus:
"O son! May you attain the glory of a warrior in battle. Having offered their dear salutations, both princes, accompanied by a great army, [set forth].

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Account of the Defeat of the Mlecchas," in the *Paumacariya*.

There the sage saw [the city] with its bodies crushed by machines and suddenly turned pale;
overcome with rage, he emitted fire along with a roar of "hum.
At that very moment, the ascetic was completely consumed by the fire of his wrath.
Because there was formerly a king named Daṇḍaka here in this region,

When time had passed, trees and various kinds of beings—such as elephants, pigs, lions, and so forth—arose in great distress. (PaumaCa. 36)

That Daṇḍaka was a great liar; having wandered through *saṃsāra* for a long time, he was reborn as a vulture and now takes his stand in the forest. Thus addressed by the ascetic: "O bird! Do not commit sinful karma."
"Do not wander again in *saṃsāra* for an infinite length of time. (PaumaCa.

In Vārāṇasī, there was a famous king named Ayala;
his wife was Śrī, who was like the goddess Śrī herself in beauty.
At the time of his meal, a monk named Sugupta arrived at her [palace].
Having been offered hospitality and seated, she asked for the sake of sons; the best of sages replied:
"O blessed lady, it is certain that two sons of beautiful conduct shall be born to you from your womb. (PaumaCa. 41–42)

Then, in due course, both of them were born as sons to Queen Śrī, beloved by the eyes of all people, possessing a splendor equal to the moon and the sun. Because they both arose as directed by the sage Sugupti, [they were named] Pauma and Camara. (PaumaCa. 43)
Then, when his father was pleased, he was given the name Sugupti.
Meanwhile, another connection arose with the city of Gandhāvatī:
two excellent princes, the sons of the royal priest of Soma. (Padma-Carita 44–45)

The first was Suketu; the second, named Agniketu, likewise became a Suketu who had taken up the state of a householder. Then, on another occasion, Suketu, through the ripening of his wholesome karma, experienced a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Having renounced the world and shaken off all impurity, he [Anantavīrya] remained in the presence of Anantavīrya.
As for the other, Agniketu, being distressed by the separation from his wife, went to Vārāṇasī and followed the dharma of an ascetic.

Having heard that his brother was intent upon the dharma of an ascetic, Suketu was moved there by affection; and for the sake of awakening him, the Guru said to Suketu, who was not yet prepared to go: "Listen now."
"That ascetic, being wicked, will engage in a dispute with you at the time of the meeting. (PaumaCa.
50) "Then, on the bank of the Nandavī river, among three women who are like daughters, she will come during the single watch of the day, dressed in a yellow garment. (PaumaCa. 51)
Knowing that such things exist among the signs, you should say to him:
