Not knowing that, the ignorant ascetic will become dejected; you should tell him about his future birth. (PaumaCa.
53) Now, in this merchant lineage, there is one named Pavara, who is filled with much wealth.
She, born from his own body, is known by the name Rucirā.
On the third day from now, she will meet her end through her own actions in the village of Kuvara,
becoming the wife of one named Viśāla.
That Māriyā, having died and become a buffalo, will die again and become a daughter of the noble Niya-māma, Santī by name.
Having spoken these words and bowed to his teacher, Sukēu then departed. (PaumaCa. 56)
Having reached the hermitage, he engaged in conversation with them. (PaumaCa.
57) Having heard everything that was taught by his preceptor and related to the ascetics, Agniketu understood that entire account. (PaumaCa. 58)
Then, at the time of her marriage, having obtained a daughter named Visālā, who was like a dispeller of darkness, Agniketu was addressed thus:
"O noble one, do not marry her; she was your daughter in a previous birth. (PaumaCa. 59)
Furthermore, her birth was recounted by Viśālapura.

Having remembered her previous birth, that maiden, overcome with intense spiritual agitation (*saṃvega*), did not desire the rite of marriage; rather, she longed only for the life of renunciation (*pravrajyā*). (PaumaCa. 60–61)

A legal dispute concerning that most excellent and extensive [matter] arose between us in the assembly hall; there was a conversation and exchange of words between the two of us. That maiden became a female ascetic, and we too heard that news.
A wife becomes a naked ascetic at the side of Anantavīrya.

Thus, through the power of delusion, women become objects of reprehensible conduct for living beings; by the power of destiny, a woman may be born as a mother, a daughter, or a sister. (Padma-Carita 63–64)
Having heard that from Jaḍāgī, he became even more terrified of the sufferings of the multitude of existences and constantly performed piteous acts for the sake of grasping the Dharma.
The sage Sugupta said to him: "O noble one! Do not cause suffering to others."
"Abandon unchaste conduct for as long as life lasts.
Practice abstinence from eating at night, avoid meat, and further cultivate the practice of fasting according to your capacity. (PaumaCa. 66–67)
Having restrained the passions, always be intent on honoring the Jina-sages;
longing for the next world, by this you shall cross over the ocean of existence.
Having taken to heart with true feeling that which was spoken by the best of sages, O King, [act accordingly].

The bird, overcome with joy, became devoted to the dharma of the lay follower (*śrāvaka*). And the son of Janaka was addressed by the ascetic: "O blessed one, this is the dharma for birds. *Padma-Carita* 69 [p. 307].
"O you of right view, protect yourself with a focused mind here in this forest. (PaumaCa.
70) Having given this instruction, the lords of sages departed for their own abodes; Sītā too, her heart filled with agitation, caressed that bird. (PaumaCa. 71)

Having heard the sound of the drum, Lakṣmaṇa, mounted upon an elephant, arrived there and beheld a heap of jewels as vast as a mountain. Then, while Lakṣmaṇa was seized by curiosity, he was addressed by Lord Rāma.
He related the entire account, beginning with the giving of alms.
"Behold the vast majesty of the Dharma in these successive existences,
by which even one such as this, though formerly a vulture, has become the color of Indra’s bow (a rainbow)."
Because his matted locks, made of jewels, gems, and gold, shone upon his head, he was called Jaḍāi by those very matted locks;
thus, endowed with humility, he stood before Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. (PaumaCariya 75)
He eats food prepared with great care and served by Sītā.
With a devoted mind, he performs the three daily salutations to the Jina together with Sītā.
Remaining close to them, the bird gazes at various other sights. (PaumaCariu 76–77)
Protected by Jananī, constantly hearing the meaning of the songs of the Jinas, dancing [in devotion],
and being devoted to the virtues of the Dharma, he became Jaḍāgī, possessed of pure majesty.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Discourse on Jaḍāgī," in the *Paumacariya*.
[The Practice of Dwelling in the Daṇḍaka Forest] Then those two sons of Daśaratha, by means of their merit from giving excellent gifts during the day...
A rain of jewels fell, and abundant merit was fully accumulated.
Furthermore, there were couches and seats made of gold, adorned with crests of gems and jewels, provided with beautiful, swaying garlands of flags. (PaumaCa. 1–2)
In that forest, they enjoy a chariot yoked with four horses that has been brought by the gods;
delighting as they please, they remain for a day, a fortnight, or even a month in enchanting locations. (PaumaCariu 3)
They remain there, having accomplished their purpose, sporting in their own natural play.
Having crossed the forest thickets and many mountains, they proceed further.
Having entered the interior of that forest, they were free from fear.

There were *vaṭa*, *dhava*, *śirīṣa*, *dhammana*, *arjuna*, *puṇnāga*, *tilaka*, and *aśvattha* trees, as well as *sarala*, *kadamba*, *ambāḍaka*, *dāḍima*, *aṅkolla*, and *billa* trees. (PaumaCa. 5–6)

Umbara, khaīra, kaviṭṭha, tenduga, bamboo, salt-trees, sāga, nimba, and jackfruit trees; mango trees and nandi-trees; thickly crowded with vauḷa, tilaya, āimuttaya, kōriṇṭaya, kuḍaya, and kujjaya trees. (PaumaCa. 7)
Its regions were adorned with *campaka*, *sahakāra* (mango), *aralu*, and *kundala* trees;
it was densely covered with *khajjūrī* (date palms), *samī*, *keyarī*, *bayarī*, *nāliērī*, and *kayalī* (plantain) trees, and especially so with *māuliṅgī* (citron) trees. (PaumaCa. 8–9)

Thus, with such various kinds of trees, it appears like the Nandana grove, beautiful in form on all sides. And there are clusters of grain, naturally grown among the *puṇḍucchuma* and other plants. *PaumaCa.* 10.5–6.
The forest shines amidst lakes whose waters are filled with lotuses and water-lilies;

it is constantly crowded with elephants, yak-cows, śarabhas, lions, boars, deer, buffaloes, and citrakas, and teeming with hundreds of deer, leopards, hyenas, tarakṣus, and bhallas. (PaumaCariu 11–12)

In some places the trees are bent down by fruit; in some places the regions are whitened by white blossoms; in some places it is blue and green; in some places there is a crimson-red luster. On the peak of Mount Daṇḍaka, there is a great elephant named Daṇḍaka.
Therefore, O moon-faced one, this Daṇḍāraṇya forest is famous among people. (PaumaCa.
14) And here too is the Kuñjaravā, a great river filled with pure water, resounding with the cries of swans, and abounding in lotuses that move at will. (PaumaCa. 15)
Seeing that excellent river, whose waves were tawny with the finest blossoms fallen from trees on both banks,
and whose eddies were tossed and churned by the constant leaping of restless dolphins and crocodiles—
seeing it, the daughter of Janaka spoke thus to Rāghava. (PaumaCariu 16)
"O one of great renown! Why do we not sport here for a moment in the water?
Having spoken thus, Rāghava descended with his beloved and bathed in the pure water, like an elephant with its mate. (PaumaCā. 17.18)
Rāghava, playing sportively, beats his water-drum, which is filled with very sweet sounds and possesses many variations,
bringing joy to his wife. Sītā,
too, there in the water, having taken fragrant white lotuses...
On the excellent neck of the beloved, she took hold of the swarms of bees that were settled there. Then those bees, struck by Rāma, began to fly about.

In Sītā’s lotus-face, they settled with the suspicion that it was a lotus; O Lord of the Lotus (Rāma), she was unable to ward off those intoxicated bees, for they were exceedingly powerful, and so the woman suddenly and firmly seized the one whose navel is a lotus (the Lord). PaumaCa. 21–22.
The bees hum as if singing songs of victory, and the birds warble like warriors; thus do living beings cling to Rāma at his bathing place.
Then, having bathed according to his desire in water cool with frost, [he was honored] by Viṣṇu.
Padmanābha crosses the river together with his beloved;
having adorned all his limbs with ornaments, Padma, seated in the pavilion of the *aimuttaka* tree, says to his younger brother: "Listen to my words. (PaumaCa. 24–25)
"Here are trees abundant with fruit, vine-arbors well-appointed, rivers with clear water, and this mountain too, filled with jewels.
Quickly bring my beloved, along with her mothers and all her kinsfolk. (PaumaCārita 26)
"Having established our camp, let us remain here in this delightful place.
Thus was he addressed by Lakṣmaṇa: "O Lord, what you have pointed out is indeed so;
it gives us confidence as well, for this is the Daṇḍaka forest itself. (Padma-Carita 27–28)
Then, while they were staying there in that forest, the summer passed away and the rainy season arrived, with its masses of thundering clouds.
The clouds, spreading across the sky, appeared like heaps of soot or dark collyrium. (PadmaCarita 29)
Having set forth, they caused the circle of the earth to be drenched by torrents that pierced through it.
(PaumaCariya 30) A most fierce wind, arising from a mass of clouds and whistling on all sides, made the clusters of trees dance as they struck one another. (PaumaCariya 31)
Blue, green, yellow, or other thick white clouds streak across the sky as they move about, their regions adorned with flashes of lightning.
The lakes, ponds, tanks, and fields were filled with fresh water, as were the flowing rivers.
Rāghava said to him, "O Prince, in such a rainy season, when the new waters are falling in abundance, your departure is certainly not appropriate. (PaumaCa. 33–34)
Having thus agreed upon this excellent dwelling, Sītā, Jaṭāyu, and Agastya joined them; Rāma and Saumitri remained there together. (PaumaCa.
Thus, finding delight in various stories, provided with food, drink, bedding, and seating,
those of pure majesty spent their time happily in the forest, which was strewn with the debris of the ocean’s shores.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Residence in the Daṇḍaka Forest," in the *Paumacariya*.
[The Chapter on the Saṃbukka Ferry] Thus,
while they were staying there, the rainy season passed away.
The autumn season itself has arrived, bestowing its splendor upon the lotus groves. (PaumaCa.
1) The sky, freed from the veil of dark clouds and washed by the rains, shines as pure as water; with the stars as its white lotuses, it bears the moon as its swan. (PaumaCa. 2)
Having attained the path of the Suhatthiya [monks] and being freed from the wind of worldly attachment, the forest groves appear as if they are dancing with their hands of tender shoots;
the warbling of birds, including swans and cranes, resounds everywhere.
In rivers and lakes, with waters filled with lotuses and water-lilies—
when such an autumn had arrived, Lakṣmaṇa, having been permitted by his elder brother, wandered through the forest and there smelled a fragrance. (PaumaCariya 4.5)
He thought to himself: "Whose is this fragrant and cool scent?
Is it from some tree hidden here, or perhaps from a god?
The Lord of Magadha asked: "O Blessed One, whose is this most excellent fragrant scent?"
Nārāyaṇa, the Great-Souled One, was himself struck with amazement by this. (PaumaCa.
7) Then Indrabhūti said: "O Śreṇika! This king of the Vidyādharas has indeed sought refuge in the second Lord of Jinas. (PaumaCa. 8)
He was named Ghaṇavāhaṇa by Bhīma, the lord of the Rākṣasas, with these words:
"Seize the city of Laṅkā from its position on the three peaks on the island of the Rākṣasas.
This is another dear secret concerning Jambūbhārata in the southern direction.
Beyond the salt ocean, there is a place situated within a cavity of the earth;
having gone half a *yojana* downward from Mount Daṇḍaka.
It shines with a vast jeweled archway reaching to the heavens from the mouth of its cave.
Having entered within it, there is a delightful and excellent city of ornaments, impregnable to enemy armies and fully equipped with all necessary implements. (Pauma-Cariya 11–12)
When this had been thus related, Meghavāhana was entreated to go to the city of Laṅkā and rule the kingdom as he desired, like Indra.
But neither the Rākṣasas nor the gods protect the island of the Rākṣasas. (PaumaCa. 13)

They were called *vijjādharas* by the people, but they were called *rākṣasas* by others. (PaumaCariya 14) Now, in the lineage of the Rākṣasas, after many high-souled lords of men who had Mehanāgas as their mounts had passed away in the course of time, (PaumaCariya 15)
There, born in the lineage of the Rākṣasas, was Rāvaṇa, the lord of three continents;
his sister was Candanakhā, whose husband was Kharadūṣaṇa.
[He was accompanied] by fourteen thousand warriors endowed with power and splendor. (PaumaCariya 16)
He enjoys Pātālapura, which is situated within a fissure in the earth, as his divine realm. (PaumaCa.
17) Kharadūṣaṇa had two sons, equal in beauty to celestial youths, named Saṃbūka and Sundana; they were the elder and the younger brothers, both of great strength. (PaumaCa. 18)
Even though he is repeatedly forbidden by his teachers and warned of death, he enters the Daṇḍāraṇya forest; for like a conch shell, he is purified by the weapon of fire. (PaumaCa.
19) He stands in the path of the range of vision of one whose application to the vows is incomplete.
"He shall become my victim here in this forest; of this there is no doubt. (PaumaCa.
20) Beyond the salt waters, near the river Koñcaravā, the crab Sambukka, having accomplished his purpose, enters the dense thicket of bamboo. (PaumaCa. 21)
Then twelve years passed, and four days remained; three days were left of the period required for the mastery of the vidyā.
At that very time, while wandering about, Lakṣmaṇa arrived at that region.

And he beheld Suyahāsa, a sword blazing with many rays, concealed by dense trees, encircled by many stones, its expanse formed upon the surface of the earth in the midst of a level ground adorned with golden lotuses. (PaumaCa. 23–24)
Lakṣmīhara quickly took that sword, which was smeared with fragrance, thickly coated with excellent saffron, and still wet from the day’s application;
he grasped it with his right hand and brandished the sword as he displayed its excellence. (PaumaCa. 25)
By him, the bamboo trunk, its roots firmly bound by a mass of creepers, was severed.
At that very moment, he saw there his head fallen, adorned with earrings, and his body smeared with a mire of blood, its limbs like coral. (PaumaCa. 26–27)
Then that son of Sumitrā, having grasped his sword, set out toward the abode of Padmaśaya;
being questioned, he related that entire account in its entirety. (PaumaCa. 28)
Candanahā went to her son’s side every single day;
then she saw his headless trunk, severed and fallen upon the surface of the earth.
Her limbs pierced by the dart of grief for her son, she fell into a swoon, and having recovered, [she wept]. (PaumaCa. 29)
"Alas, my son! You who were so fond of quarreling, you now weep, your tears having released their flow.
You remained for twelve years with your mind fixed on the highest yoga; yet for four days and three nights more, you were not spared by the God of Death. (PaumaCa. 30–31)
What wrong have I done, O cruel path of karma, that my son—who was a treasury of many virtues—has been snatched away from me so untimely?
Or rather, by whom has my son been struck down through my own lack of merit? (PaumaCariu 32)
This is the fruit of that karma; there is no doubt about it. (PaumaCa.
33) O son, all those desires which were conceived by me, being devoid of merit, have all been quickly overturned by destiny in a contrary manner. (PaumaCa. 34)
Taking her son’s words to heart, she kisses him—his body smeared with the mire of blood—as if it were water; with wide-open eyes, she utters piteous lamentations.
Having lamented for a long time, she harbors wrath toward that terrifying forest.
Candanakhā wanders about, swiftly searching for her enemy. (PaumaCa.
36) Wandering there, upon seeing both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, her limbs pierced by the arrows of love, she abandons both anger and sorrow. (PaumaCa. 37)
At that very moment, having conceived a desire for them, she thought, "I shall go; whom among them shall I choose? Then, having adorned herself, she quickly arrived in their presence. (PaumaCa. 38)
Shedding tears from her eyes, she sat down at the foot of a *puṇṇāga* tree.
Seeing her, the daughter of Janaka seized that girl by the hair with her hand and said:
"Stay in our presence; do not be afraid. (PaumaCa. 39–40)
And Rāghava said to her: "Who are you, young woman!
Why do you wander alone here in this forest, so terrible and frequented by lions and other beasts?
She replied: "In my home, my beautiful mother has passed away."
He too, through grief for her, met his death. (PaumaCa.
42) Seized by sin and abandoned by my kinsmen, I, having attained detachment, have come here to the Daṇḍaka forest. (PaumaCa. 43)
"Somewhere while wandering, I have seen you here by the power of my merit;
be clearly my refuge, for I am without refuge and filled with suffering. (PaumaCa. 44)
Then she, fallen under the power of passion, having offered her salutation, said to the descendant of Raghu:
"O one of great fame, have it so that I do not lose my life!
Having heard these words, the two of them signaled to one another.
Avoiding contact with other young women, they did not even exchange a word with her.
Having spoken much and heaving long, hot sighs, she stepped aside from them and quickly went to her own place. (PaumaCariu 46–47)

He, Vimalaprabhāva, out of a desire to seek her marks, caused a battle to be waged through the instruction of others; having become enamored of the beauty and virtues of that celestial maiden, he returned once again.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, named "The Forest of Śambūka," in the *Paumacariya*.
[The Chapter on Rāma’s Lamentation during Sītā’s Abduction] There she weeps in the palace, her sandalwood paste washed away by the flowing tears.
With her face, cheeks, and thighs wounded, her hair disheveled and soiled with dust, she was seen by Khara and Dūṣaṇa like a crushed lotus plant. Then the Lord of Beasts (Rāvaṇa) said to her:
"Tell us, by whom has this suffering been inflicted upon you? (PaumaCa. 1–2)
Then Candanā said: "O son, I went in search of you, but I saw only you in the forest, fallen upon the earth with your head severed.
Someone wicked has killed my son, that hero."
He took the perfected spell, the celestial bow, and the great sword.
As for me, having placed that son’s head upon my lap, my limbs scorched by grief, I wept in the forest like a doe deprived of her fawn, with my eyes flowing with tears.
At that very moment, O Lord, I was embraced by that wicked man who harbors enmity toward his own son;
while I was weeping, he held me tightly for some purpose or other.
Though I was unwilling, I was seized by that evil one by my teeth and my nails.
"I reached such a state, all alone in battle. (PaumaCa.
7) "But even from that, I was protected by the power of merit produced in a previous existence;
with my conduct unbroken, I have somehow come here, O Lord. (PaumaCa. 8)
"O Dūṣaṇa! Rāvaṇa, the king of the Vidyādharas and lord of three continents, is my brother;
you too are my husband, yet even so, I have encountered this suffering. (PaumaCārita 9)
Having heard her words,
Khara-dūṣaṇa, his mind overwhelmed with grief, went there and saw his son fallen on the ground, pale and lifeless. Filled with rage and resentment, he returned to his own home in an instant.

Equipped with six thousand excellent warriors clad in armor, he [Rāvaṇa] was then addressed by Citraprabha, the minister of the Lord of Laṅkā: "Send a messenger to him on this mission. (PaumaCa. 11–12)
Then Kharadūṣaṇa, having dispatched a messenger to Rāvaṇa,
wept with eyes streaming from his arms, overcome by the grief of not seeing his son.
While the messenger was still reporting [the news], Rāvaṇa delayed for a long time.
Dūṣaṇa set out with fourteen thousand warriors. (PaumaCa.
14) Hearing the roar of Dūṣaṇa’s army in the sky, Sītā cried out, “What is this? What is this? and clung to Rāma. (PaumaCa. 15)
"Do not fear, O moon-faced one! These swans flying through the sky are uttering cries from their mouths;
lower your bow, and I shall drive them away. (Padma-Carita 16) And at that moment, a great army, crowded with various weapons, arrived nearby.
Seeing it spreading across the sky like a mass of clouds, Rāmadeva thought:
"Could these be the gods who, having gone to Nandīśvara, are now returning to their own abodes? (PaumaCa. 17–18)

"Or perhaps he who was slain in battle for the sake of uprooting his enemies has been cut down at the base of the family tree; have these kinsmen come for him? Surely it is because of that wicked woman, having gone to her, that this has happened. (PaumaCariya 19)
"Since he has abandoned his seat and departed, they have come here because of him.
Having reflected thus, Rāma, casting his gaze with his bow and arrow ready toward Lakṣmaṇa, said: "Listen to these words. (PaumaCa. 20–21)
"O Rāghava! Since I am peaceful, it is not fitting for you to fight me now; protect this daughter of Janaka. I shall go to face the enemies. (PaumaCā.
22) Just as a lion, surrounded by his foes, lets out a roar, so do I release [this cry].
"At that very moment, O Rāghava, come quickly and without hesitation!
Having spoken thus, he then put on his armor, took up his weapons and shield, and engaged in battle simultaneously with the Rākṣasa warriors. (PaumaCārita 23.24)
Upon Lacchīhara, the clouds released a multitude of raindrops in various formations, like a mountain discharging a torrent of waterfalls. (PaumaCa. 25)
Having warded off the multitude of weapons released by the moon-like rays [of his enemies] in battle, Lakṣmīhara discharges arrows with a speed like the staff of Yama;
[he whose head is] adorned with a noble crown and excellent earrings of blazing jewels and gems. (PaumaCā. 26)
Severed by arrows that match their [auspicious] marks, heads fall like lotuses.
Elephants and horses collapse, as do warriors and chariots with their banners in disarray, their limbs crushed and uttering terrible cries. (PaumaCariya 27–28)
Having reached this interval, Daśagrīva, seated in his flower-palace, intent on killing and deeply agitated, let out a roar like a thundercloud.
Then, while driving [his chariot] toward the southern direction, he beheld Sītā, the cause of his delusion. (PaumaCārita 29)
With limbs beautiful in every part, she was like the wife of the Lord of the Gods in her form. (PaumaCa.
30) His body scorched by the fire of passion, the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, with a single-minded focus, reflected:
"What is the use of this kingdom to me here, if I am deprived of her? (PaumaCa. 31)
Having reflected thus, Daśamukha then, by means of the *avalokanā* vidyā, knows their names, their conduct, and their lineage:
"This one who fights alongside many in battle is Lakṣmaṇa. (PaumaCa. 32)
"Rāma is indeed staying here in the forest together with Sītā. (PaumaCa.
33) "Leaving him at the front of the battle, I shall swiftly carry off Sītā, who utters a lion’s roar like the sound of Lakṣmaṇa’s arrows, thereby deceiving Rāma as well. (PaumaCa. 34)
"Both of these will surely be slain, along with Khara and Dūṣaṇa and their entire army.
Having reflected thus, the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa) let out a lion’s roar. Hearing that lion’s roar, which was clearly articulated with distinct syllables, Rāma—*PadmaCariya 35*.
Then, his mind becoming agitated, he struck his excellent bow.
"Wait here for a moment, O beautiful one! Protected by the matted locks of Jaṭāyu, remain near Lakṣmaṇa until I have gone and returned. (PaumaCa. 36–37)
Having spoken thus, that supreme one, though being restrained by the evil omens,
rushed with speed toward the front of the battle where the warriors raised a tumultuous roar. At that very moment, the Ten-faced one suddenly descended from the sky.
The daughter of Janaka was captivated by him like a lotus on the arms of an intoxicated elephant.
Though she was the wife of her lord, she could not be carried off; for the enraged Jaṭāyu struck the ten-faced Rāvaṇa on his broad chest with his talons and claws. (PaumaCariya 39–40)
Enraged by that killing of his bird, the Ten-faced One (Rāvaṇa), out of indignation toward birds,
quickly struck it down upon the surface of the earth, its limbs pulverized by the blow of his hand. (PaumaCariya 41)

Three [types of] wind, five [types of] dust, and five unsurpassed hells.

Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one—

Furthermore, they are repeatedly torn apart, their bodies cut and split by thorny brambles.

With their limbs pierced by swords, spears, javelins, lances, and tridents,

Thus, in this sequence, those who have reached the hells within the earth-worlds experience great suffering for a vast duration of time, finding not even a moment’s taste of happiness. (PaumaCa. 83–84)
Whatever sufferings there are in the three worlds, such as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, all those a living being with heavy karma experiences in hell.
Therefore, hear this: the fruit of unrighteousness is most intensely painful.
With hearts full of praise for the Dharma and striving in the religion of the Supreme Jina, the gods dwelling in the upper celestial abodes of the Ratnaprabhā realm reside eternally.

Sixty-four, eighty-four, sixty-two, as well as ninety-six, seventy-six, and sixty-seven lakhs—these are the numbers for the remaining six [classes of gods] as well.

Earth, fire, water, wind, and vegetation are the immobile beings. (PaumaCārita 92)

On its southern and northern sides, all the Kulaparvatas touch the salt water on both parts; they consist of excellent gold and jewels. (PaumaCa. 103–104)

The Northern Devakuru regions, headed by the Śālmalī and Jambū trees.

The happiness of humans is indeed greater than that of the lords of men;

Likewise, the bliss of the inhabitants of the celestial abodes (bhavanavāsin) is superior; that of the gods dwelling in the kalpas is greater still; the bliss of the gods of the Graiveyakas is even more so; and the bliss of the Anuttara gods is infinite. But as for the transmigrating soul, pleasure derived from touch and the other senses is certainly caused by delusion and is, from its very root, nothing but suffering. (PaumaCa. 173–174)

"Those fortunate ones who delight in the words of the Jina, who are endowed with knowledge, conduct, and vision,

One who has destroyed the fault of attachment practices penance, having restrained the flow of the senses through right vision;

Right conduct consists of non-violence, truthfulness, and the avoidance of what belongs to others, as well as celibacy (*brahma*).

194) One whose resolve is firm through energy, who is constantly engaged in the sixteen-fold restraint...

Hearing that, Vasudatta became enraged; clad in blue garments and holding a sharp sword in his hand, he went to where the merchant was staying at night. On the following day, the merchant remained in the garden, standing with his face turned toward the teacher.

The deer that arose there are those whom I previously inhabited. For her sake, however, those Kurangas, having slaughtered one another in the terrible forest, were born as tigers through the influence of their karma. (PaumaCariya 18–19)

102) Five hundred years, increased by thirty years of the Duṣama age, had passed since Vīra attained liberation (siddhi); after that, this biography was composed. (PaumaCa. 103)
For those who consume poison and eat snakes, and who are attached to the bait of sense-objects by the lure of women, war is the ultimate [consequence];
deluded by passion, he did not attain tranquility despite thousands of young women. (PaumaCā. 104)

That king of the Vidyādharas went to hell with his soul unrestrained (PaumaCa. 105). He, who was pampered by countless devoted women yet never reached satiety—how then could another be satisfied by a few scanty women? (PaumaCa. 106)
Those men who are attached to the pleasures of the senses and devoid of austerity, restraint, and self-control, are fools who, having abandoned a jewel, take up a mere cowrie shell.
Having heard this account concerning the cause of enmity involving another's wife... [PaumaCariu 10.7]
O fool, prepare for the next world; otherwise, you shall surely face ruin.
By the fruit of well-performed deeds, a human being attains a station that is a treasure-house of great prosperity;
and by the fruit of ill-performed deeds, one meets with an evil fate—such is the natural law in this world. (PaumaCa. 108–109)
No one gives anything to anyone else; likewise, even though the gods in the world do not bestow health, wealth, or long life, why then are so many suffering?
In this Purāṇa, all things—desire, worldly existence, dharma, and liberation—are described.
Abandoning faults, take up virtues, O you who produce joy in the heart! (PaumaCa.
111) What is the use of much speaking in this world, which only brings distress? Understand even from a single word and always delight in the doctrine of the Jina. (PaumaCa. 112)
O you who delight in the teachings of Viṣṇu, become devoted to the supreme Dharma so that you may attain it without obstacle; there, Baladeva and others have gone. (PaumaCa. 11)

May all the deities of the sacred traditions (samayadevatās) certainly carry out this practice of Rahula, which is worthy of praise, together with people endowed with self-restraint; as well as the world of those destined for liberation, and all the planets beginning with the Sun without exception. (PaumaCa. 114)
With minds as serene as the full moon and with intellects devoted to the dharma of the supreme Jinas—
O wise ones, may you always forgive whatever errors I have committed here through the fault of negligence, and may you fulfill that for me. (PaumaCariya 115–116)
The teacher named Rāhu, who had grasped the true nature of both his own tradition and other traditions, was invincible;
his disciple was Vijaya, who brought joy to the lineage of the Nāila clan.
This *Rāghavacarita* was composed by the scholar Vimala, the son of that [Vijaya]. *PaumaCa.* 117.
Having heard the former lives of Nārāyaṇa and Śrī,
those gods who were free from envy and whose minds were permeated by devotion to them—
may they grant me the stainless awakening through the life-stories of these great beings. (PaumaCariya 118–119)
Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Departure of Padmanīrvaṇa," in the *Paümacariya*.
Thus is completed the *Paümacariya*, composed by the great sage Vimalācārya Puṣpadanta, who was a disciple of the sun-like Rāhusūri of the Nāila lineage.
